units.title: Chemistry of life, biomolecules and enzymes
units.summary: Levels of organization, atoms and bonds, characteristics of life, water, the four macromolecules, and how enzymes work.

notes.title: Organization of living things
notes.html:
Levels of organization

  • Smallest to largest: atom → molecule → cell → tissue → organ → organ system → organism → population → community → ecosystem → biosphere.
  • The cell is the most important level: it's the smallest thing that is alive.
  • Population = one species in an area. Community = all the populations living together. Ecosystem = the community plus the nonliving environment (water, soil, air).
  • An emergent property shows up at a higher level that the parts don't have alone. One minnow swims aimlessly; a group of minnows schools.

Classifying life

  • Three domains: Bacteria, Archaea, Eukarya. Six kingdoms: Eubacteria, Archaebacteria, Protista, Plantae, Fungi, Animalia (the last four are all Eukarya).
  • LUCA is the last universal common ancestor. Carl Woese defined Archaea in 1977 using 16S ribosomal RNA.
  • Taxonomy levels: Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species ("King Philip Came Over For Great Soup"). Species is the most specific.
  • Plants and fungi use division instead of phylum.

notes.title: Atoms and chemical bonding
notes.html:
Atoms

  • Atoms are the smallest unit of matter. Protons (+) and neutrons (no charge) are in the nucleus; electrons (−) are in shells around it.
  • Atomic number = protons. Atomic mass = protons + neutrons. In a neutral atom, electrons = protons.
  • Isotopes have the same protons but different neutrons (C-12 has 6 neutrons, C-14 has 8). Radioisotopes are used in PET scans, radiation therapy and carbon dating.
  • Shells: the inner one holds up to 2 electrons, outer shells up to 8. Only the outer electrons interact with other atoms.

Bonds

  • Covalent bond: electrons are shared. Equal sharing = nonpolar (O2, CH4). Unequal sharing = polar (H2O).
  • Ionic bond: electrons are transferred, making ions that attract (Na gives one electron to Cl → Na+ and Cl−).
  • Hydrogen bonds are weak attractions between molecules, like the δ+ H of one water molecule and the δ− O of another.
  • One line in a structure = single bond (one shared pair). Two lines = double bond.

notes.title: Characteristics of life
notes.html:
The 7 characteristics

  • Order, response to stimuli, reproduction, growth and development, regulation, homeostasis, energy processing.
  • Responses can be positive (toward) or negative (away). Phototaxis = light, chemotaxis = chemicals, geotaxis = gravity.
  • Asexual reproduction = one parent, identical offspring (binary fission, strawberry runners). Sexual = two parents. All reproduction passes on DNA.
  • Autotrophs make their own food (plants, algae). Heterotrophs eat other things (animals, fungi, yeast).

Homeostasis and feedback

  • Homeostasis = keeping a stable internal environment. It's a dynamic equilibrium: the body constantly adjusts. It takes energy.
  • Negative feedback reverses a change back to the set point. Example: eat pizza → blood glucose rises → pancreas releases insulin → cells take in glucose, liver stores it as glycogen → glucose drops → insulin stops.
  • Positive feedback pushes further in the same direction. Example: childbirth, where oxytocin makes contractions stronger and stronger.
  • Ghrelin makes you hungry; leptin suppresses appetite after a meal.
  • Endotherms make their own body heat (penguins) and need more food. Ectotherms rely on the environment (lizards bask in the sun).

notes.title: Central dogma
notes.html:
• The central dogma: DNA → RNA → protein.
  • DNA → RNA is transcription. RNA → protein is translation.
  • A codon is three mRNA bases that code for one amino acid. RNA uses uracil (U) instead of thymine, so A pairs with U.
  • Changing one DNA base can change a codon, which can change one amino acid. That changes the protein's primary structure, its folding, and its function. Sickle cell disease comes from one amino acid change in hemoglobin.

notes.title: Properties of water
notes.html:
Why water is special

  • Water is polar: oxygen pulls the shared electrons, so the O side is δ− and the H sides are δ+. That lets water molecules hydrogen bond to each other.
  • Cohesion = water sticks to water. Adhesion = water sticks to other things. Surface tension lets a water strider walk on water. Cohesion and adhesion pull water up plants.
  • Ice floats: hydrogen bonds lock ice into an open lattice, so it's less dense than liquid water. Floating ice insulates lakes so fish survive.
  • High heat capacity: water heats and cools slowly, keeping bodies and coastal climates stable.
  • High heat of vaporization: evaporating water takes a lot of heat with it, which is why sweating cools you.
  • Water is a great solvent. Salt dissociates into Na+ and Cl−; the δ− O end faces Na+ and the δ+ H ends face Cl−. Oil is nonpolar (hydrophobic), so it doesn't mix.

Acids, bases and pH

  • Water dissociates into H+ (forms hydronium, H3O+) and OH−.
  • Acids add H+ (HCl). Bases add OH− (NaOH).
  • The pH scale runs 0 to 14 and 7 is neutral. Lower pH = more acidic. Lemon juice is about 2, pure water 7, seawater about 8, bleach about 12 to 13.
  • Neutralize an acid with a base. For acid on skin, flush with lots of cool running water.

notes.title: Big picture: building and breaking macromolecules
notes.html:
• Biological macromolecules are large molecules needed for life, built from smaller organic molecules. Organic means they contain carbon bonded to hydrogen.
  • The four classes: carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, nucleic acids.
  • Monomer = single unit. Polymer = many units bound together. All macromolecules follow the same pattern: monomer + monomer + monomer ... = polymer.
  • Dehydration synthesis builds. An H from one monomer and an OH from the other leave as a water molecule, and the monomers join with a covalent bond. Think "put together while losing water."
  • Hydrolysis breaks. Water is added and splits the bond; one piece gets the H, the other gets the OH. Think "split with water."
  • Both reactions are sped up by enzymes, and each macromolecule has its own specific enzyme.
  • Why carbon: a carbon atom has 6 protons and 6 electrons, with 4 electrons in its outer shell. That lets it form 4 covalent bonds, so it can build long chains, branches and rings. That's why it's the backbone of every macromolecule.

notes.title: Carbohydrates
notes.html:
What you need to know
  1. Distinguish mono-, di- and polysaccharides. Give examples of each and recognize structural formulas.
  2. How carbs are used in plants and animals for energy storage.
  3. How carbs are used in plants and animals as structure.

Basics

  • Made of C, H, O in a 1:2:1 ratio: (CH2O)n. So carbon to hydrogen is 1:2. "Carbo" + "hydrate" = carbon + water.
  • Three types: monosaccharides, disaccharides, polysaccharides.

Monosaccharides: simple ring sugars

  • Most common one: glucose, formula C6H12O6. Others: fructose, galactose.
  • Names usually end in -ose.
  • By number of carbons: pentose = 5 carbons (example: ribose), hexose = 6 carbons (glucose, fructose, galactose).
  • Glucose, fructose and galactose are isomers: same formula (C6H12O6), different arrangement of atoms. Glucose and galactose are 6-sided rings; fructose is a 5-sided ring.
  • Glucose gets broken down in cellular respiration to make ATP. Plants make glucose from CO2 and water, and store the extra as starch.

Disaccharides: two monosaccharides combined

  • Formed by dehydration synthesis between two monosaccharides. The covalent bond between them is a glycosidic bond.
  • Sucrose = glucose + fructose. Table sugar, the most common disaccharide.
  • Lactose = glucose + galactose. Milk sugar.
  • (Maltose = glucose + glucose. Shows up again in Ch 6 when amylase breaks down starch.)

Polysaccharides: long chains of monosaccharides

Linked by glycosidic bonds. Two jobs: storing energy and building structure.

PlantsAnimals
Energy storageStarch: mix of amylose and amylopectin (both glucose polymers). Stored in roots and seeds.Glycogen: the animal version of starch. Stored in liver and muscle cells.
StructureCellulose: makes up plant cell walls.Chitin: makes up exoskeletons of insects and crustaceans.
  • Starch is in seeds as food for the embryo when the seed germinates.
  • Amylase (in saliva) is the enzyme that breaks starch into smaller sugars like maltose and glucose.
  • When blood glucose drops, glycogen is broken down to release glucose.
  • Humans can't digest cellulose. Grazing animals (cows, etc.) digest it thanks to bacteria and protists in their gut that make the enzyme cellulase.
  • Fiber (mostly cellulose) in your diet: keeps bowel movements regular, regulates how fast blood glucose gets used, and helps remove excess cholesterol.

notes.title: Lipids
notes.html:
What you need to know
  1. Compare saturated to unsaturated fats.
  2. List the functions of lipids.
  3. Identify a steroid from a picture (4 rings).
  4. Identify the main component of the cell membrane and what about that molecule is significant.
  5. Why are triglycerides technically not "polymers"? Think about dehydration synthesis of a fat.

What lipids are

  • Nonpolar and hydrophobic (insoluble in water). Nonpolar means the molecule has no charged ends because it's mostly C–C and C–H bonds, so it doesn't mix with water.
  • Functions: long-term energy storage (fat), insulation, waterproof covering and protection (waxes), cell membranes (phospholipids), hormones (steroids).
  • Types on the slides: fats and oils, waxes, phospholipids, steroids.

Fats and oils (triglycerides)

  • Made of glycerol + fatty acids. A triglyceride = 1 glycerol + 3 fatty acids, joined by dehydration synthesis, which releases 3 water molecules.
  • Why it's not a true polymer: it isn't a chain of repeating monomers. It's always just 3 fatty acids hooked onto one glycerol, so it can't keep growing like a polymer does.
  • In animals, fat is stored in cells called adipocytes.

Saturated vs unsaturated

SaturatedUnsaturated
BondsOnly single bonds (no double bonds); max hydrogensOne or more double bonds
ShapeStraight, packs tightlyDouble bond makes a kink, can't pack tightly
Room tempSolid (butter, lard)Liquid (oils)
ExamplesPalmitic acid, stearic acidLinoleic acid, oleic acid; olive, corn, canola, cod liver oil

Cis vs trans fats

  • Cis: the H's at the double bond are on the same side, causing the kink (oleic acid).
  • Trans: the H's are on opposite sides, so the chain stays straight like a saturated fat (elaidic acid).
  • Trans fats come from artificially hydrogenating oils in the food industry (margarine, shortening).
  • Banned in many places because they raise LDL ("bad" cholesterol), which leads to plaque in arteries and heart disease.
  • Omega-3 fatty acids: essential (your body can't make them, you have to eat them). Sources: fish like salmon, trout, tuna.

Waxes

  • Mainly covering and protection. Being hydrophobic, wax keeps water from sticking: it waterproofs aquatic birds' feathers and leaf surfaces.

Phospholipids

  • The main structural component of the cell membrane.
  • Structure: glycerol + 2 fatty acids + a phosphate group.
  • Amphipathic: has a hydrophilic head (phosphate, water loving) and hydrophobic tails (fatty acids, water fearing).
  • In the membrane they form a bilayer: heads face the water inside and outside the cell, tails hide in the middle. That's the "significant" thing about them.

Steroids

  • Made of 4 fused carbon rings. That's how you spot one in a picture.
  • Examples: cholesterol and sex hormones estrogen and testosterone.
  • Grouped with lipids because they're hydrophobic / insoluble in water. Different because they're rings, not fatty acid chains on glycerol.
  • Cholesterol: essential part of animal cell membranes, sits between phospholipids, keeps the membrane's integrity and fluidity. It lets animal cells (a) not need a cell wall, (b) change shape, (c) move freely.

notes.title: Proteins
notes.html:
What you need to know
  1. Amino acid structure.
  2. Levels of protein structure (including bonding).
  3. Functions of proteins.
  4. How environmental conditions impact proteins.
  5. Examples of proteins.

What proteins are and what they do

  • Polymers of amino acids joined by peptide bonds. Also called polypeptides.
  • Mainly building blocks for living tissue, and they form a huge variety of shapes.
  • Examples from the slide: lactase (enzyme), hemoglobin, insulin, keratin, myoglobin (muscles).
  • Functions: support, enzymes, transport, defense, hormones, motion.
  • Enzymes are catalysts for biochemical reactions and are specific to their substrate. A catabolic enzyme breaks down its substrate (amylase breaks down starch).
Type (reading guide / Table 3.1)ProteinJob
DigestiveAmylaseBreaks down starch
TransportHemoglobin (also albumin)Carries substances in the blood
StructuralKeratin, actin, tubulinBuilds structures like the cytoskeleton
DefenseImmunoglobulinsProtects from foreign pathogens
ContractileActin, myosinMuscle contraction
HormoneInsulinRegulates blood glucose

Amino acid structure

  • A central carbon (the alpha carbon) bonded to four things: an amine group (NH2), a carboxyl group (COOH), an H, and an R group (side chain).
  • Every amino acid has the NH2 and COOH. They differ only in the R group, which determines the amino acid's chemical and physical properties (polarity, acidity).
  • There are 20 amino acids.
  • Essential amino acids can't be made by the body, so you must get them from your diet. Example: tryptophan.
  • Aromatic amino acids have a ring in the R group (tryptophan, phenylalanine; the guided learning also uses histidine).
  • R group with a hydroxyl (–OH) is polar: it can make hydrogen bonds, so it's hydrophilic. Serine has one; valine (just CH3 groups) doesn't.
Fix this on your worksheetOn slide 3 you put carbon as the element behind methionine's unique properties. It's sulfur. Every amino acid has carbon; the S is what's special about this R group.

Peptide bonds

  • Amino acids join by dehydration synthesis. The OH comes from the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the H comes from the amino group of the other. Together they leave as H2O.
  • The peptide bond forms between the C (of the C=O) and the N.
  • Dipeptide = 2 amino acids. Tripeptide = 3 amino acids, made with 2 peptide bonds and 2 waters released. Rule: n amino acids = n − 1 peptide bonds = n − 1 waters.
  • A polypeptide has an N terminal (free amino group) at one end and a C terminal (free carboxyl group) at the other.

The four levels of structure

LevelBonds / interactionsWhat it is
PrimaryCovalent peptide bondsThe specific sequence of amino acids in the chain
SecondaryHydrogen bonds between backbone C=O and N–HLocal folding into alpha helices and beta pleated sheets
TertiaryR group interactions: hydrophobic interactions, hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, disulfide bondsOverall 3D shape of one polypeptide chain
QuaternaryInteractions between the chains (hydrophobic, H bonds, ionic)Two or more polypeptide chains assembled into one working protein

Primary. Every protein has a unique sequence, written with one-letter codes. Myoglobin has 154 amino acids and starts M G L S = methionine, glycine, leucine, serine. Change one amino acid and the protein can break: sickle cell disease is one amino acid swap in the beta chain of hemoglobin (glutamic acid replaced by valine). The hemoglobin then forms long fibers that bend red blood cells into a sickle shape.

Secondary. The chain folds locally because of hydrogen bonds. Two shapes: alpha helix (coil) and beta pleated sheet (zigzag folds side by side).

Tertiary. The helix or pleat folds into a 3D shape. The four bond types:

  • Hydrophobic interactions: nonpolar R groups tuck toward the center to avoid water.
  • Hydrophilic interactions: polar R groups face outward toward water. (Hydrogen bonds form between polar groups.)
  • Ionic bonds: oppositely charged R groups attract.
  • Disulfide bonds (bridges): covalent bonds between the S atoms of two cysteines.

Myoglobin is a tertiary structure example: one chain, 154 amino acids, alpha helices and no beta sheets, with a heme group (with iron) in the middle that holds oxygen. It stores oxygen in muscle.

Double-check this answerYou wrote 6 alpha helices. The purple picket-fence model on this slide labels the helices A through H, which is 8, and myoglobin is normally described as having 8 helices. Count them yourself on the image and ask your teacher if the key says 6.

Quaternary. More than one polypeptide chain. Hemoglobin carries oxygen in blood and has 4 polypeptide chains, each with its own heme group (iron), so 4 hemes.

Denaturation

  • A protein that is denatured loses its shape, and so loses its function. The amino acid sequence (primary structure) stays the same.
  • Caused by heat, changes in pH, or chemicals. Sometimes reversible, sometimes not (frying an egg white).
  • Shape is everything: an enzyme binds its specific substrate at its active site, so if the shape changes, it can't bind.

Cytochrome c (reading guide, Evolution Connection)

  • Found in the mitochondria. Human cytochrome c has 104 amino acids. Comparing its sequence between species gives clues about evolutionary relationships and a common ancestor. (Humans and chimps: identical. Humans and rhesus monkeys: 1 difference.)

notes.title: Nucleic acids
notes.html:
What you need to know
  1. Nucleotide structure (including classifying bases).
  2. Structural differences between DNA and RNA.
  3. Anti-parallel nature.
  4. Overall function.
  • Information storing molecules. Most important macromolecules for the continuity of life because they carry the cell's genetic blueprint (instructions) and get passed from parent to offspring.
  • Two kinds: DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) and RNA (ribonucleic acid).
  • Monomer: the nucleotide. Each nucleotide = a sugar (deoxyribose or ribose, a 5-carbon sugar) + a phosphate + a nitrogen base.

Bases

PurinesPyrimidines
Rings2 rings1 ring
BasesAdenine, guanineCytosine, thymine (DNA), uracil (RNA)
"Pure As Gold": purines are A and G. Pyrimidines are the "CUT" ones: C, U, T.
  • DNA bases: A, T, G, C. RNA bases: A, U, G, C (uracil replaces thymine).
  • Base pairing rule: A with T (A with U in RNA), G with C. A purine always pairs with a pyrimidine. Pairs are held by hydrogen bonds.

Structure

  • DNA is a double helix. The sugar-phosphate backbone is on the outside; base pairs are on the inside like steps of a staircase.
  • Antiparallel: the two strands run in opposite directions. The 5′ end of one strand lines up with the 3′ end of the other.
  • Sugar difference: ribose (RNA) has an OH on its 2nd carbon; deoxyribose (DNA) has just an H there. "Deoxy" = missing an oxygen.
  • RNA is usually single-stranded.

Where it lives and what it does (reading guide)

  • DNA is in the nucleus of eukaryotes (and in mitochondria and chloroplasts). In prokaryotes it's not enclosed in a membrane.
  • The cell's entire genetic content = its genome.
  • In eukaryotes, DNA + histone proteins form chromatin.
  • RNA is mostly involved in protein synthesis. Types: mRNA, rRNA, tRNA, microRNA. The smallest is microRNA (miRNA).
  • A set of three bases = a codon (codes for one amino acid).
  • DNA → RNA is transcription. RNA → protein is translation.
  • Writing complementary RNA: swap each base for its partner, using U for A. DNA AATTGC → RNA UUAACG.
DNARNA
SugarDeoxyriboseRibose
BasesA, T, G, CA, U, G, C
StrandsDouble helixUsually single
JobStores genetic infoProtein synthesis
LocationStays in nucleusLeaves the nucleus

notes.title: Testing for biomolecules
notes.html:
• Iodine tests for starch: it turns blue-black if starch is there.
  • Benedict's solution tests for simple sugars (like glucose and maltose): heated, it changes from blue to green, yellow, orange or red when sugar is present.
  • Biuret tests for protein: blue turns purple/violet.
  • Lipids: rub on brown paper and look for a see-through grease spot, or use Sudan III (red layer).
  • Example: mix starch with amylase. Afterward, iodine barely changes color (the starch is gone) and Benedict's turns positive (amylase made maltose).

notes.title: Energy and metabolism
notes.html:
The hook: milk

  • 10,000 years ago, nobody past infancy could digest lactose (milk sugar). Babies could, but lost the ability after infancy. Adult animals can't digest milk, which is why you shouldn't give adult cats milk.
  • Essential questions: (1) What cellular mechanisms allow for the digestion of milk? (2) Why do some adult humans keep this ability? Answers at the end of the Enzymes section.
  • Lactose (disaccharide) + water → lactase → glucose + galactose (monosaccharides). That's hydrolysis.

Metabolism basics

  • Bioenergetics = energy flow through living systems.
  • Metabolism = the sum of all chemical reactions in a cell / organism.
  • Breaking down glucose (cellular respiration): C6H12O6 + 6O2 → 6CO2 + 6H2O + energy
  • Photosynthesis is the reverse: plants use sunlight energy to turn CO2 into sugar (glucose).
  • ATP (adenosine triphosphate) is the cell's energy currency.
  • Making 1 glucose from 6 CO2 takes 18 ATP and 12 NADPH. Breaking down 1 glucose yields 36 to 38 ATP.
  • The first organisms used anaerobic metabolism because the early atmosphere had no oxygen.
  • Every step of a metabolic pathway is helped along by a protein called an enzyme.

Catabolic vs anabolic

CatabolicAnabolic
Does whatBreaks down large, complex molecules into smaller onesBuilds complex molecules from simple raw materials
EnergyReleases energyUses (requires) energy
TypeExergonic, degradationEndergonic, synthesis
EquationAB → A + B + energyA + B → AB
ExampleBreaking down glucose (cellular respiration)Making glucose from CO2 (photosynthesis), proteins from amino acids, DNA from nucleotides
Cats break things = catabolic. Anakin built the Death Star = anabolic.

Types of energy

  • Energy = the ability to do work.
  • Kinetic energy = energy of motion. Potential energy = stored energy (a ball held up, water behind a dam).
  • When the ball drops, potential energy converts to kinetic.
  • Potential energy stored in chemical bonds = chemical energy.
  • Energy is one of the BIG IDEAS: biological systems use free energy and molecular building blocks to grow, reproduce and maintain dynamic homeostasis.

Laws of thermodynamics

  • Thermodynamics = the study of energy and energy transfer involving matter.
  • First law (conservation of energy): energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred or transformed.
  • Second law: in a closed system, entropy (randomness / disorder) tends to increase over time. Also: heat flows from higher temperature to lower. Every energy transfer loses some energy as unusable heat, so no transfer is 100% efficient.
  • Heat energy = energy transferred that isn't doing work.
  • So why don't living things fall into chaos? They're open systems with a constant energy input, ultimately from the sun.
  • Living organisms need energy for: metabolism, homeostasis, movement and activity, growth and development, reproduction.

Free energy and ΔG

  • Gibbs free energy (G) = usable energy, available to do work after entropy is accounted for.
  • During energy transfer some energy becomes unusable, such as heat.
  • Enthalpy (ΔH) = the total energy change of the system.
  • Formula: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS (T = temperature in Kelvin, ΔS = change in entropy)
ExergonicEndergonic
EnergyReleases energyRequires / absorbs energy
ΔGNegative (< 0)Positive (> 0)
Spontaneous?Yes (spontaneous doesn't mean fast; rusting is slow)No (non-spontaneous)
Graph"Downhill": products lower than reactants"Uphill": products higher than reactants
PathwayCatabolicAnabolic
ExamplesCombustion, making table salt (sodium + chlorine), chemiluminescence, breaking down glucosePhotosynthesis, a chick developing from an egg, melting ice

From the reading guide's Quick Reference: endergonic = non-spontaneous, absorbs energy from the surroundings, free energy of the system increases, ΔG positive; exergonic = spontaneous/favorable, releases energy to the surroundings, the new bonds formed are stronger than the ones broken, free energy decreases, ΔG negative, randomness of the system increases.

  • Most chemical reactions are reversible (true).
  • Activation energy = the initial energy needed to get a reaction started. Even exergonic reactions need it.
  • Molecules contorted right before bonds break are in the transition state (high energy, unstable).
  • Heating a system makes reactants react faster.
  • Catalysts lower the activation energy. ΔG is unchanged.

ATP

  • ATP = adenosine bound to three phosphate groups.
  • ATP → ADP + energy is a hydrolysis reaction (water breaks off the last phosphate). It's exergonic.
  • Energy coupling: the energy from ATP hydrolysis powers an endergonic process. Membrane example: the sodium-potassium pump.
Heads upYour OpenStax doc skips section 6.4 (ATP), so these three ATP answers are the standard textbook answers, not from your doc. Reading guide questions 35-37 ask about them.

notes.title: Enzymes
notes.html:
What enzymes are

  • An enzyme is a protein molecule that acts as an organic catalyst to speed up reactions. It does this by lowering the activation energy.
  • Properties: made of proteins; speed up reactions; unchanged after each reaction (reusable); specific to their substrate.
  • Enzymes do not change ΔG. They can't make an endergonic reaction exergonic.
  • Substrate = the reactant the enzyme attaches to. Active site = where on the enzyme the substrate binds. Together they make the enzyme-substrate complex.
  • Energy of activation = the energy required to cause the reaction.
  • Naming: most enzyme names end in -ase, usually named after the substrate. Sucrose → sucrase. Lactose → lactase.
EnzymeActionWhere
LactaseLactose (milk) to simple sugarsSmall intestine
AmylaseStarch to simple sugarsSaliva
PepsinProteins to amino acidsStomach
LipaseFats to fatty acidsPancreas / intestine
Alcohol dehydrogenaseAlcohol to non toxic substances and sugarLiver / stomach

Milk digestion

  • Lactose = galactose + glucose joined by a glycosidic bond.
  • Lactase lowers the energy needed to break the bond. The simple sugars then get absorbed by cells of the small intestine.
  • Lactase has 4 subunits of 1023 amino acids each, 4092 total, so it's a quaternary structure.

How enzymes work

  • Induced fit model: substrate and enzyme fit together. The slide says it's also called the "lock and key model."
  • Degradation = breaking down (one substrate → smaller products). Synthesis = building (substrates combined → bigger product).
Know both versionsYour slide treats induced fit and lock and key as the same thing. OpenStax says lock and key is the older idea (a rigid perfect fit), and induced fit is the updated one: the enzyme's shape shifts slightly when the substrate binds to get the ideal fit. If a question asks about the difference, that's it.

Activation energy graphs

  • Enzymes lower the activation energy (the hump) but don't change the free energy (ΔG) of the reaction (start and end heights stay the same).
  • On a graph: activation energy = from reactants up to the peak. ΔG = difference between reactants and products.

Factors affecting enzyme speed

  • Four factors: substrate concentration, temperature, pH, enzyme concentration.
  • Optimum temperature or pH = where the enzyme reacts fastest.
  • Enzymes can be denatured: they change shape so much they no longer work. High temperature or extreme pH causes it.
  • To increase rate: add more substrate, add more enzyme, move temperature or pH toward the optimum.

Siamese cats: their enzyme tyrosinase only works at lower temperatures. Below 33°C it's active and makes dark pigment; above 33°C it's inactive. So the cooler parts (nose, ears, tail, paws) are darker. Proof that temperature controls enzyme activity.

Enzyme regulation

  • Competitive inhibition: the inhibitor binds to the active site and blocks the substrate. ("If it fits, it sits.")
  • Allosteric (noncompetitive) inhibition: the inhibitor binds to another site (the allosteric site) and changes the enzyme's shape, so the substrate can't bind.
  • Allosteric activation: an activator binds the allosteric site and changes the shape so the enzyme binds substrate more efficiently.
  • Feedback inhibition: the product of a pathway becomes an inhibitor, slowing or stopping more product from being made. On the slide, the final product inhibits enzyme 1 at its allosteric site.
  • The most common source of coenzymes (organic helper molecules enzymes need) is dietary vitamins.

Enzymes in action and labs

  • Catalase breaks down hydrogen peroxide: 2H2O2 → 2H2O + O2. You can see it working from the oxygen bubbles.
  • Amylase activity: measure the maltose produced from breaking down starch, or use iodine to test whether starch is still there.
  • To measure reaction speed: (A) measure how much product is made (oxygen), or (B) measure how much substrate (hydrogen peroxide) is left when you stop the reaction.
  • The oxygen graph levels off because the substrate (H2O2) has been used up; there's nothing left to convert.
  • Testing lactase: measure the glucose produced from lactose (or use the yeast-balloon setup below).

Can yeast digest lactose? (experiment design)

  • Yeasts are single-celled fungi and are heterotrophs. They eat sugar and make CO2 (why bread rises).
  • Setup: flasks with glucose, sucrose, lactose, lactose + lactase, and a control, each with a balloon on top, left 24 hours.
  • Balloons: catch the CO2. Bigger balloon = more sugar the yeast used.
  • Control: yeast + water, no sugar.
  • Independent variable: the type of sugar (and whether lactase was added). Dependent variable: the amount of CO2 (balloon size).
  • Reading it: if the lactose balloon stays flat but lactose + lactase inflates, the yeast can't make lactase on its own.
NoteThe slide only asks these questions. The answers above are the logical ones for this setup; check them against what your class concluded.

Back to the essential questions

  • What cellular mechanism allows milk digestion? The enzyme lactase in the small intestine hydrolyzes lactose into glucose and galactose, which get absorbed.
  • Why do some adults keep it? They're lactase persistent: they keep making lactase after infancy (the HHMI "Got Lactase?" film covers the mutation behind this).
  • Lactose intolerant: no lactase, so lactose passes to the large intestine where bacteria ferment it, making gas and acids → diarrhea, abdominal pain, gas, bloating.

questions.q: Which level of organization is the smallest that is actually alive?
questions.explain: Cells are the smallest unit that can carry out all the characteristics of life. Molecules aren't alive.

questions.q: All the zebras, lions and acacia trees living in one savanna make up a:
questions.explain: Several different species living together is a community. Add the soil, water and air and it becomes an ecosystem.

questions.q: Which taxonomic level is the most specific?
questions.explain: Species is the most specific level. King Philip Came Over For Great Soup ends at species.

questions.q: Fungi, Plantae, Animalia and Protista all belong to which domain?
questions.explain: All four are eukaryotic kingdoms in domain Eukarya.

questions.q: Carbon has atomic number 6 and mass 14 in carbon-14. How many neutrons does it have?
questions.explain: Neutrons = mass − atomic number = 14 − 6 = 8.

questions.q: In a polar covalent bond, electrons are:
questions.explain: Unequal sharing makes one end slightly negative and the other slightly positive, like in water.

questions.q: When sodium and chlorine form NaCl, what happens?
choices: They share a pair of electrons
Sodium transfers an electron to chlorine
Chlorine transfers an electron to sodium
questions.explain: Sodium gives one electron to chlorine, making Na+ and Cl−, which attract in an ionic bond.

questions.q: What holds one water molecule to the water molecule next to it?
questions.explain: Covalent bonds are inside one water molecule. Hydrogen bonds are the weak attractions between molecules.

questions.q: A marathon runner sweats to cool down. Which characteristic of life is this?
questions.explain: Sweating keeps body temperature stable, which is homeostasis.

questions.q: Contractions getting stronger during childbirth is an example of:
questions.explain: Oxytocin makes contractions stronger, which causes more oxytocin. It keeps going in the same direction, so it's positive feedback.

questions.q: Cockroaches run away when the kitchen light turns on. This is:
questions.explain: They move away from light: negative phototaxis.

questions.q: Which organism is an autotroph?
questions.explain: Algae make their own food from sunlight. Mushrooms and yeast are fungi, which are heterotrophs.

questions.q: After you eat, which hormone does the pancreas release to lower blood glucose?
questions.explain: Insulin lets cells take in glucose and the liver store it as glycogen, bringing blood glucose back down.

questions.q: The process of making RNA from DNA is called:
questions.explain: DNA → RNA is transcription. RNA → protein is translation.

questions.q: A DNA strand reads TAC. What is the complementary mRNA codon?
questions.explain: T pairs with A, A pairs with U (RNA has no T), C pairs with G: AUG.

questions.q: How many bases make up one codon?
questions.explain: A codon is three bases that code for one amino acid.

questions.q: Why does ice float on liquid water?
choices: Hydrogen bonds lock ice into an open, less dense lattice
Ice has a higher heat capacity
questions.explain: Stable hydrogen bonds hold ice molecules farther apart, so ice is less dense than liquid water.

questions.q: Sweating cools you off mainly because water has a high:
questions.explain: Breaking hydrogen bonds to evaporate water takes a lot of heat, and that heat leaves your skin with the sweat.

questions.q: A solution with pH 3 is:
questions.explain: Below 7 is acidic. pH 3 has more H+ than OH−.

questions.q: Water climbing up thin tubes in a plant stem depends on:
questions.explain: Adhesion pulls water up the tube walls and cohesion pulls the chain of water molecules along behind.

questions.q: When salt dissolves in water, which part of a water molecule faces the Na+ ion?
choices: Neither, Na+ doesn't interact with water
questions.explain: Opposite charges attract, so the slightly negative oxygen end faces the positive Na+.

questions.q: Why can carbon form the backbone of so many large molecules?
choices: It has 4 outer electrons and can form 4 covalent bonds
It's the heaviest element in cells
It has no electrons in its outer shell
questions.explain: Four bonds let carbon make long chains, branches and rings.

questions.q: Dehydration synthesis:
questions.explain: An H and an OH leave as water, and the monomers join with a covalent bond.

questions.q: Digesting a protein into amino acids is an example of:
questions.explain: Breaking a polymer into monomers by adding water is hydrolysis.

questions.q: Sucrose (table sugar) is made of:
questions.explain: Sucrose = glucose + fructose. Lactose = glucose + galactose. Maltose = glucose + glucose.

questions.q: Animals store extra glucose as:
questions.explain: Glycogen is stored in liver and muscle cells. Starch is the plant version.

questions.q: Which carbohydrate makes up insect exoskeletons?
questions.explain: Chitin is structural in animals like insects and crustaceans. Cellulose is structural in plant cell walls.

questions.q: Glucose, fructose and galactose all have the formula C6H12O6. They are:
questions.explain: Same formula, different arrangement of atoms means they're isomers.

questions.q: A fatty acid with no double bonds between carbons is:
questions.explain: Saturated means every carbon is full of hydrogens, with only single bonds. The tail is straight.

questions.q: Why are unsaturated fats usually liquid at room temperature?
choices: Their kinked tails can't pack tightly
questions.explain: Cis double bonds put kinks in the tails, so the molecules can't pack closely and stay liquid.

questions.q: In a phospholipid, which part is hydrophilic?
questions.explain: The phosphate head faces water. The fatty acid tails are hydrophobic and face inward in a membrane.

questions.q: Cholesterol, estrogen and testosterone are all:
questions.explain: Steroids are lipids built from four fused carbon rings.

questions.q: The monomer of a protein is:
questions.explain: Amino acids link by peptide bonds to form polypeptides.

questions.q: What makes one amino acid different from another?
questions.explain: All amino acids share the same backbone. The R group gives each one its properties.

questions.q: The alpha helices and beta pleated sheets in a protein are its:
questions.explain: Secondary structure is folding held together by hydrogen bonds along the backbone.

questions.q: Hemoglobin is made of four polypeptide chains. That's an example of:
questions.explain: Quaternary structure means more than one polypeptide chain working together.

questions.q: A protein heated to very high temperature loses its shape and stops working. This is called:
questions.explain: Denaturing changes the protein's shape, so it can't do its job.

questions.q: A nucleotide is made of:
choices: A sugar, a phosphate group and a nitrogenous base
An amino group and a carboxyl group
questions.explain: Sugar + phosphate + base. In DNA the sugar is deoxyribose; in RNA it's ribose.

questions.q: Which base is found in RNA but not DNA?
questions.explain: RNA uses uracil in place of thymine.

questions.q: In DNA, adenine pairs with:
questions.explain: A pairs with T and C pairs with G in DNA.

questions.q: Which test would show that starch is present?
questions.explain: Iodine turns blue-black with starch.

questions.q: You mix starch with amylase and wait. Which result shows amylase worked?
choices: Benedict's test turns positive for sugar
questions.explain: Amylase breaks starch into maltose, a sugar, so Benedict's turns positive and the iodine reaction fades.

questions.q: A food sample turns biuret purple. Which biomolecule is present?
questions.explain: Biuret turns from blue to purple when protein is present.

questions.q: Iodine stays orange-brown, Benedict's turns orange, biuret stays blue, and there's a grease spot on brown paper. What's in the food?
questions.explain: Only Benedict's (sugar) and the brown paper (lipid) were positive.

questions.q: All the chemical reactions in a cell together are called:
questions.explain: Metabolism includes both building (anabolic) and breaking down (catabolic) reactions.

questions.q: Building large molecules from small ones is:
questions.explain: Anabolic pathways build up and require energy. Catabolic pathways break down and release energy.

questions.q: A reaction that releases energy is:
questions.explain: Exergonic reactions release energy. Endergonic reactions need energy put in.

questions.q: What is activation energy?
choices: The energy released by a reaction
The energy needed to get a reaction started
questions.explain: Every reaction needs a starting push. Enzymes lower that activation energy.

questions.q: Which molecule is the cell's main energy currency?
questions.explain: ATP releases energy when its last phosphate bond is broken, powering cell work.

questions.q: Enzymes speed up reactions by:
choices: Being used up in the reaction
questions.explain: Enzymes lower activation energy and are not used up, so they can be reused.

questions.q: The part of an enzyme where the substrate binds is the:
questions.explain: The substrate fits into the active site, like a key into a lock, and the enzyme shifts to grip it (induced fit).

questions.q: Lactase breaks down lactose. What is the substrate?
questions.explain: The substrate is what the enzyme acts on. Enzyme names often end in -ase, sugars in -ose.

questions.q: A competitive inhibitor works by:
choices: Binding to the active site and blocking the substrate
Breaking the enzyme into amino acids
questions.explain: It competes with the substrate for the active site. Noncompetitive inhibitors bind somewhere else and change the enzyme's shape.

questions.q: Pepsin works best around pH 2. At pH 8 it would most likely:
choices: Slow down or stop because it denatures
questions.explain: Each enzyme has an optimum pH. Far from it, the active site changes shape and the enzyme can denature.

questions.q: Adding more enzyme to a reaction with plenty of substrate will usually:
questions.explain: More enzyme means more active sites working at once, so the rate goes up as long as substrate isn't limiting.

questions.q: Which pairing of macromolecule and monomer is correct?
questions.explain: Carbs are built from monosaccharides, proteins from amino acids, nucleic acids from nucleotides.

questions.q: Lactase is an enzyme. Which macromolecule class is it?
questions.explain: Nearly all enzymes are proteins, which is why heat and pH can denature them.

questions.q: Fill in the Biomolecule Building Blocks table (slide 1): for each class give the monomer, examples, and job.
questions.a:

questions.q: What are biological macromolecules?
questions.a: Large molecules necessary for life, built from smaller organic (carbon-containing) molecules.

questions.q: Name the four classes of macromolecules.
questions.a: Carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, nucleic acids.

questions.q: Monomers combine to create ____. What's the difference between the two?
questions.a: Polymers. A monomer is a single unit; a polymer is many units bound together.

questions.q: What happens during dehydration synthesis? What bond forms?
questions.a: Two monomers join. An H from one and an OH from the other leave as H<sub>2</sub>O, and a covalent bond forms between them. It builds polymers.

questions.q: What happens during hydrolysis?
questions.a: Water is added to break a polymer into monomers. One piece gets an H, the other gets an OH. It breaks polymers.

questions.q: What can speed up dehydration synthesis and hydrolysis?
questions.a: Enzymes (specific ones for each macromolecule).

questions.q: What about the carbon atom makes it ideal for life?
questions.a: It has 4 outer electrons, so it forms 4 covalent bonds. That lets it build chains, branches and rings: a stable backbone for large molecules.

questions.q: Slide matching (a carbohydrate, b lipid, c protein, d nucleic acid): 1 contains adenine and thymine, 2 lactose, 3 chains of amino acids, 4 long term energy storage, 5 cholesterol, 6 chains of fatty acids and glycerol, 7 plant cell walls.
Ratio of carbon to hydrogen to oxygen in carbohydrates?
questions.a: 1:2:1, written (CH<sub>2</sub>O)n. Carbon to hydrogen alone is 1:2.

questions.q: Most common monosaccharide? Most monosaccharide names end in what?
questions.a: Glucose. -ose.

questions.q: Chemical formula for glucose?
questions.a: C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub>

questions.q: Glucose is used during [cellular respiration / photosynthesis]. Excess glucose is stored as [protein / starch].
questions.a: Cellular respiration. Starch (in plants).

questions.q: Example of a pentose? A hexose?
questions.a: Pentose (5 C): ribose. Hexose (6 C): glucose (also fructose, galactose).

questions.q: Why are glucose and fructose considered isomers?
questions.a: Same chemical formula (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub>) but different structure (arrangement of atoms).

questions.q: For these three hexoses: (a) molecular formula of each? (b) same formula, different structure is called? (c) why "hexoses"?
questions.a: (a) All three are C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub>. (b) Isomers. (c) Each has 6 carbons.

questions.q: How are disaccharides formed? What's the bond called?
questions.a: Two monosaccharides join by dehydration synthesis (water released). The covalent bond is a glycosidic bond.

questions.q: Name two common disaccharides and their monomers. Which is most common?
questions.a: Sucrose (glucose + fructose) and lactose (glucose + galactose). Sucrose (table sugar) is the most common.

questions.q: What is a polysaccharide?
questions.a: A long chain of monosaccharides linked by glycosidic bonds.

questions.q: Starch is made from a mixture of ____ and ____.
questions.a: Amylose and amylopectin.

questions.q: Why is starch found in seeds?
questions.a: It's stored food for the embryo when the seed germinates.

questions.q: What is amylase?
questions.a: An enzyme (in saliva) that breaks starch down into smaller sugars like maltose and glucose.

questions.q: How do animals store glucose? Where?
questions.a: As glycogen, the animal equivalent of starch, stored in liver and muscle cells.

questions.q: What is a plant's cell wall made from?
questions.a: Cellulose.

questions.q: How do grazing animals break down cellulose?
questions.a: Bacteria and protists living in their digestive system secrete the enzyme cellulase, which breaks cellulose into glucose.

questions.q: What carbohydrate makes up insect and crustacean exoskeletons?
questions.a: Chitin.

questions.q: Which are benefits of carbs (fiber) in the diet? Reduces cholesterol in blood / Promotes regular bowel movements / Reduces sugar circulating in blood / Reduces risk of breast cancer.
questions.a: Check the first three. Fiber removes excess cholesterol, keeps bowel movements regular, and regulates blood glucose. Breast cancer isn't mentioned, so leave it unchecked.

questions.q: Energy storage carb in plants vs animals? Structural carb in plants vs animals?
questions.a: Storage: starch (plants), glycogen (animals). Structure: cellulose (plant cell walls), chitin (exoskeletons).

questions.q: Lipids tend to be [polar / nonpolar] and [soluble / insoluble] in water.
questions.a: Nonpolar, insoluble (hydrophobic).

questions.q: What does nonpolar mean?
questions.a: No charged or partially charged ends (mostly C–C and C–H bonds), so it doesn't interact with water. Hydrophobic.

questions.q: List the functions of lipids (at least 2 for the worksheet, all for the slide list).
questions.a: Long-term energy storage, insulation, covering/protection (waxes), cell membranes (phospholipids), hormones (steroids).

questions.q: Two main components of a fat molecule?
questions.a: Glycerol and fatty acids.

questions.q: Fatty acid with only single bonds is ____; with a double bond is ____.
questions.a: Saturated; unsaturated.

questions.q: Unsaturated fats are [solid / liquid] at room temperature. Why?
questions.a: Liquid. Double bonds kink the chains so they can't pack tightly.

questions.q: Compare saturated and unsaturated fats (bonds, shape, room temp, example).
questions.a: Saturated: single bonds only, straight, solid (butter, palmitic/stearic acid). Unsaturated: at least one double bond, kinked, liquid (oils, linoleic/oleic acid).

questions.q: What type of cells store fat in animals?
questions.a: Adipocytes.

questions.q: Examples of unsaturated fats?
questions.a: Olive oil, corn oil, canola oil, cod liver oil (vegetable oils).

questions.q: Why are trans fats banned in some places?
questions.a: They raise LDL ("bad" cholesterol), which causes plaque in arteries and heart disease. They're made by artificially hydrogenating oils.

questions.q: Where would you get omega-3 fatty acids?
questions.a: Fish: salmon, trout, tuna. (Your body can't make them.)

questions.q: Why do aquatic birds and leaves have a waxy covering?
questions.a: Wax is hydrophobic, so it keeps water off (waterproofing and protection).

questions.q: Where are phospholipids found?
questions.a: The cell (plasma) membrane. They're its main structural component.

questions.q: Why are phospholipids called amphipathic?
questions.a: They have a hydrophilic part (phosphate head) and a hydrophobic part (fatty acid tails).

questions.q: How do phospholipids arrange in the membrane, and why does that matter?
questions.a: As a bilayer: heads face the water inside and outside the cell, tails face each other in the middle away from water.

questions.q: How many carbon rings are in a steroid?
questions.a: 4 fused rings.

questions.q: Why are steroids grouped with lipids? What makes them different?
questions.a: Grouped because they're hydrophobic/insoluble in water. Different because they're built from fused rings, not fatty acid chains.

questions.q: Two examples of steroids?
questions.a: Cholesterol, testosterone, estrogen (any two).

questions.q: What does cholesterol do in the membrane, and what 3 things does it let animal cells do?
questions.a: Keeps membrane integrity and fluidity. Lets animal cells (a) not need a cell wall, (b) change shape, (c) move freely.

questions.q: Why are triglycerides technically not polymers?
questions.a: They aren't chains of repeating monomers. Dehydration synthesis just attaches 3 fatty acids to 1 glycerol (releasing 3 waters), and it stops there.

questions.q: Proteins are polymers of ____ joined by ____ bonds. Other name for proteins?
questions.a: Amino acids, peptide bonds. Polypeptides.

questions.q: List the six protein functions from the slide.
questions.a: Support, enzymes, transport, defense, hormones, motion.

questions.q: Give 5 examples of proteins from the slides.
questions.a: Lactase, hemoglobin, insulin, keratin, myoglobin (also amylase, immunoglobulins).

questions.q: Enzymes are ____ for biochemical reactions. What is a catabolic enzyme?
questions.a: Catalysts. An enzyme that breaks down its substrate.

questions.q: Match: amylase, hemoglobin, keratin, immunoglobulins to: a protect from pathogens, b structural, c digestive breaks down starch, d transport in blood.
questions.a: Amylase c, hemoglobin d, keratin b, immunoglobulins a.

questions.q: Name the protein: transports substances in blood / builds the cytoskeleton / protects from pathogens / muscle contraction.
questions.a: Hemoglobin (or albumin) / actin or tubulin / immunoglobulins / actin and myosin.

questions.q: Draw a generic amino acid. Label all four things on the central carbon.
questions.a: Central C bonded to: amine group (NH<sub>2</sub>), carboxyl group (COOH), H, and R group (side chain).

questions.q: What do all amino acids have in common, and what differs?
questions.a: All have NH<sub>2</sub>, COOH (and H on the central C). They differ in the R group, which defines each one.

questions.q: The nature of an amino acid (polarity, acidity) is determined by what?
questions.a: Its R group (side chain).

questions.q: How many amino acids are there?
Why are some amino acids "essential"? Example?
questions.a: The body can't make them, so they have to come from your diet. Tryptophan.

questions.q: Which element in methionine's side chain gives it unique properties?
questions.a: Sulfur.

questions.q: What makes an amino acid aromatic? Name two.
questions.a: A ring in its R group. Tryptophan, phenylalanine (histidine on the guided learning).

questions.q: Leucine, isoleucine, phenylalanine: which is least like the others and why?
questions.a: Phenylalanine. Its R group is a ring; the other two are branched carbon chains.

questions.q: Valine vs serine: how alike, how different, which is hydrophilic and why?
questions.a: Both have an amine and carboxyl group; their R groups differ. Serine is hydrophilic because its R group has a hydroxyl (–OH), which is polar and can hydrogen bond.

questions.q: Making a dipeptide: what reaction, and where does the water come from?
questions.a: Dehydration synthesis. OH from the carboxyl group of one amino acid + H from the amino group of the other.

questions.q: The peptide bond forms between which two atoms?
questions.a: The C of the C=O and the N.

questions.q: A tripeptide forms how many peptide bonds and waters? A 9 amino acid chain like bradykinin?
questions.a: Tripeptide: 2 and 2. Bradykinin: 8 peptide bonds (n − 1).

questions.q: The N terminal has a free ____ group; the C terminal has a free ____ group.
questions.a: Amino (NH<sub>2</sub>); carboxyl (COOH).

questions.q: What are the four levels of protein structure?
questions.a: Primary, secondary, tertiary, quaternary.

questions.q: The sequence of amino acids is the ____ structure. What bonds hold it?
questions.a: Primary. Covalent peptide bonds.

questions.q: First four amino acids of myoglobin (MGLS)?
questions.a: Methionine, glycine, leucine, serine.

questions.q: Sickle cell anemia is caused by a single change in what protein chain? What does the change make hemoglobin do?
questions.a: The beta chain of hemoglobin (glutamic acid swapped for valine). Hemoglobin forms long fibers that distort red blood cells into a sickle shape.

questions.q: The two secondary structures, and the bond that holds them?
questions.a: Alpha helix and beta pleated sheet. Hydrogen bonds between backbone C=O and N–H.

questions.q: The 3D structure of one protein chain is its ____ structure. Name the 4 bond types involved.
questions.a: Tertiary. Hydrophobic interactions, hydrogen bonds (hydrophilic interactions), ionic bonds, disulfide bonds.

questions.q: The nature of the R groups causes the protein to [fold / dismantle].
questions.a: Fold.

questions.q: Where do hydrophobic vs hydrophilic R groups end up in a folded protein?
questions.a: Hydrophobic toward the center (away from water). Hydrophilic on the outside (toward water).

questions.q: What is a disulfide bond, and between which amino acid?
questions.a: A covalent bond between the S atoms of two cysteines.

questions.q: Quaternary structures are formed from several ____. Example?
questions.a: Polypeptide chains (subunits). Hemoglobin: 4 chains.

questions.q: Myoglobin vs hemoglobin: alike and different?
questions.a: Alike: proteins with alpha helices and iron-containing heme groups that bind O<sub>2</sub>. Myoglobin: 1 chain, 1 heme, tertiary, stores O<sub>2</sub> in muscle. Hemoglobin: 4 chains, 4 hemes, quaternary, carries O<sub>2</sub> in blood.

questions.q: What happens when a protein is denatured? What can cause it?
questions.a: It loses its shape and therefore its function (sequence stays the same). Heat, pH changes, chemicals.

questions.q: Enzymes bind to a specific ____.
questions.a: Substrate (at the active site).

questions.q: Cytochrome c: where is it, how many amino acids in humans, and what can differences in it tell us?
questions.a: Mitochondria. 104. Evolutionary relationships and a common ancestor (not protein function).

questions.q: Why are nucleic acids important for the continuity of life?
questions.a: They carry the genetic blueprint/instructions for the cell and are passed from parent to offspring.

questions.q: Where is DNA found?
questions.a: Nucleus of eukaryotes (also mitochondria and chloroplasts). Not membrane-enclosed in prokaryotes.

questions.q: The cell's entire genetic content is its ____. In eukaryotes, DNA + histones form ____.
questions.a: Genome. Chromatin.

questions.q: RNA is mostly involved in what cellular process?
questions.a: Protein synthesis.

questions.q: DNA and RNA are made of what monomers? Three parts of each?
questions.a: Nucleotides. Sugar (5-carbon), phosphate, nitrogenous base.

questions.q: Four bases in DNA?
questions.a: Adenine, thymine, guanine, cytosine.

questions.q: Purines have [2/1] rings; pyrimidines have [2/1]. Which bases are which?
questions.a: Purines 2 rings: adenine, guanine. Pyrimidines 1 ring: cytosine, thymine, uracil.

questions.q: Sugar in DNA? In RNA? What's the difference?
questions.a: Deoxyribose; ribose. Ribose has an OH on the 2nd carbon; deoxyribose has an H there (one less oxygen).

questions.q: Shape of DNA? What's on the outside vs inside?
questions.a: Double helix. Sugar-phosphate backbone outside, base pairs inside.

questions.q: Base pairing rule?
questions.a: A–T (A–U in RNA) and G–C. Purine with pyrimidine, held by hydrogen bonds.

questions.q: What does antiparallel mean?
questions.a: The two DNA strands run in opposite directions: one 5′ to 3′, the other 3′ to 5′.

questions.q: DNA = A A T T G C. Complementary RNA?
questions.a: U U A A C G

questions.q: A set of three bases is called a ____.
questions.a: Codon.

questions.q: Smallest of the four types of RNA?
questions.a: MicroRNA (miRNA).

questions.q: DNA dictates RNA through ____. RNA dictates protein through ____.
questions.a: Transcription. Translation.

questions.q: List 4 structural differences between DNA and RNA.
questions.a: Sugar (deoxyribose vs ribose), base (T vs U), strands (double vs usually single), job/location (stores info in nucleus vs protein synthesis, leaves nucleus).

questions.q: The concept of energy flow through living systems is called?
questions.a: Bioenergetics.

questions.q: All the chemical reactions inside cells (or an organism) is called?
questions.a: Metabolism.

questions.q: Equation for breaking down glucose?
questions.a: C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub> + 6O<sub>2</sub> → 6CO<sub>2</sub> + 6H<sub>2</sub>O + energy

questions.q: In photosynthesis, plants use sunlight to convert ____ into ____.
questions.a: CO<sub>2</sub> into sugar (glucose).

questions.q: Energy currency of the cell?
questions.a: ATP.

questions.q: What's needed to make 1 glucose from 6 CO<sub>2</sub>? How much ATP comes from breaking down 1 glucose?
questions.a: 18 ATP and 12 NADPH. 36 to 38 ATP.

questions.q: Pathways that require energy and build molecules are ____. Pathways that release energy and break molecules down are ____.
questions.a: Anabolic. Catabolic.

questions.q: The first organisms evolved ____ metabolism. Why?
questions.a: Anaerobic. The early atmosphere had no oxygen.

questions.q: Example of an anabolic pathway?
questions.a: Making sugar from CO<sub>2</sub> (photosynthesis), or building proteins from amino acids, or DNA from nucleotides.

questions.q: What type of protein facilitates each reaction step?
questions.a: An enzyme.

questions.q: Catabolic vs anabolic: give the energy, ergonic type, equation and memory trick for each.
questions.a: Catabolic: breaks down, releases energy, exergonic, AB → A + B + energy, "cats break things." Anabolic: builds, uses energy, endergonic, A + B → AB, "Anakin built the Death Star."

questions.q: How is energy defined? Energy of motion vs stored energy?
questions.a: The ability to do work. Kinetic vs potential.

questions.q: When a held ball drops, potential energy converts to ____. Potential energy in chemical bonds is called ____.
questions.a: Kinetic. Chemical energy.

questions.q: What is Gibbs free energy?
questions.a: Usable energy available to do work, after the energy lost to entropy is accounted for.

questions.q: During energy transfer, some energy becomes an unusable form such as ____.
questions.a: Heat.

questions.q: What is enthalpy? Formula for ΔG?
questions.a: The total energy change of the system (ΔH). ΔG = ΔH − TΔS.

questions.q: If energy is released, ΔG is ____ and the reaction is ____. If energy is required, ΔG is ____ and the reaction is ____.
questions.a: Negative, exergonic. Positive, endergonic.

questions.q: Anabolic processes are [endergonic / exergonic]. Catabolic are [endergonic / exergonic]. Which ones are spontaneous?
questions.a: Anabolic endergonic. Catabolic exergonic. Exergonic reactions are spontaneous.

questions.q: Example of an endergonic process from Fig 6.8?
questions.a: A chick developing from a fertilized egg.

questions.q: Two examples each of endergonic and exergonic reactions (quick reference).
questions.a: Endergonic: photosynthesis, melting ice. Exergonic: combustion, sodium + chlorine making table salt, chemiluminescence.

questions.q: True or false: most chemical reactions are reversible.
questions.a: True.

questions.q: The initial energy needed to start a reaction is the ____ energy. A contorted molecule about to break bonds is in the ____ state.
questions.a: Activation. Transition.

questions.q: Heating a system makes reactants react [faster / slower].
questions.a: Faster.

questions.q: Catalysts [raise / lower] activation energy. ΔG is [greater / less / unchanged] in catalyzed reactions.
questions.a: Lower. Unchanged.

questions.q: Thermodynamics is the study of ____.
questions.a: Energy and energy transfer involving matter.

questions.q: First law of thermodynamics?
questions.a: Energy can't be created or destroyed, only transferred or transformed (conservation of energy).

questions.q: Second law of thermodynamics (both ways the slide says it)?
questions.a: In a closed system, entropy (disorder) tends to increase over time. Or: heat flows from higher temperature to lower temperature.

questions.q: In the food chain slide, the plant gets 10 J from 1000 J of sunlight. Where did 990 J go, and which law explains it?
questions.a: Lost to the environment as heat. Second law (no transfer is 100% efficient). The first law says it wasn't destroyed.

questions.q: Heat energy is energy that transfers without ____. The amount of disorder in a system is ____.
questions.a: Doing work. Entropy.

questions.q: If entropy always increases, why don't living systems fall into chaos?
questions.a: They're open systems getting a constant input of energy, ultimately from the sun.

questions.q: Laws of thermodynamics, biology edition: three things organisms must do?
questions.a: (1) Obtain energy from surroundings (sun, food, chemicals). (2) Transform it into usable energy (ATP). (3) Lose some as heat during transfer.

questions.q: Five things living organisms need energy for?
questions.a: Metabolism, homeostasis, movement and activity, growth and development, reproduction.

questions.q: ATP is adenosine bound to ____. What reaction turns ATP into ADP + energy?
questions.a: Three phosphate groups. Hydrolysis.

questions.q: Energy coupling occurs in what process on the membrane?
questions.a: The sodium-potassium pump.

questions.q: What are enzymes made of? What do they do to activation energy?
questions.a: Proteins. Lower it.

questions.q: List the four properties of enzymes from the slide.
questions.a: Made of proteins; speed up reactions; unchanged after each reaction (reusable); specific to substrate.

questions.q: True or false: enzymes change ΔG of the reaction.
questions.a: False. They lower activation energy only.

questions.q: The reactants enzymes bind to are ____. The location where they bind is the ____.
questions.a: Substrates. Active site.

questions.q: True or false: enzymes are specific to their substrates. Enzymes are unchanged and reusable.
questions.a: True. True.

questions.q: What enzyme breaks down sucrose? Lactose? What ending do most enzyme names have?
questions.a: Sucrase. Lactase. -ase.

questions.q: Fill the enzyme table: lactase, amylase, pepsin, lipase, alcohol dehydrogenase. Action and where.
questions.a: Lactase: lactose to simple sugars, small intestine. Amylase: starch to simple sugars, saliva. Pepsin: proteins to amino acids, stomach. Lipase: fats to fatty acids, pancreas/intestine. Alcohol dehydrogenase: alcohol to non toxic substances and sugar, liver/stomach.

questions.q: Lactose is made of what two sugars joined by what bond? Where are the products absorbed?
questions.a: Galactose and glucose, glycosidic bond. Cells of the small intestine.

questions.q: How many subunits does lactase have, and what level of structure is that?
questions.a: 4 (1023 amino acids each, 4092 total). Quaternary.

questions.q: What is the induced fit model? How is it different from lock and key?
questions.a: Substrate and enzyme fit together, with the enzyme shifting shape slightly as the substrate binds. Lock and key is the older idea of a rigid, perfect fit. (Your slide calls them the same thing.)

questions.q: Degradation vs synthesis enzyme reactions?
questions.a: Degradation: substrate broken into smaller products. Synthesis: substrates combined into a larger product.

questions.q: Four factors that affect enzyme speed?
questions.a: Substrate concentration, temperature, pH, enzyme concentration.

questions.q: List three things that can increase the rate of an enzymatic reaction.
questions.a: More substrate, more enzyme, temperature or pH moved toward the optimum.

questions.q: What is the optimum temperature or pH?
questions.a: Where the enzyme has its fastest reaction rate.

questions.q: What can cause an enzyme to denature? What happens when it does?
questions.a: High temperature or extreme pH. It changes shape so much it no longer works (substrate can't bind).

questions.q: Why are Siamese cats darker on their nose and ears?
questions.a: Their enzyme tyrosinase only works at lower temperatures (below 33°C). Those body parts are cooler, so pigment is made there.

questions.q: Checkpoint: match A, B, C to X (change in free energy ΔG), Y (activation energy without enzyme), Z (activation energy with enzyme).
questions.a: A = Y (activation energy without enzyme, up to the black peak). B = Z (activation energy with enzyme, up to the red peak). C = X (ΔG, reactants down to products).

questions.q: On an energy graph, how can you tell exergonic from endergonic?
questions.a: Exergonic: products end lower than reactants (downhill). Endergonic: products end higher (uphill).

questions.q: Identify the type of inhibition for Enzyme A and Enzyme B.
questions.a: Enzyme A: competitive (inhibitor in the active site). Enzyme B: noncompetitive / allosteric (inhibitor on another site changes the shape).

questions.q: What is competitive inhibition?
questions.a: An inhibitor binds the active site and blocks the substrate.

questions.q: What is allosteric inhibition? Sketch it.
questions.a: An inhibitor binds a different site (allosteric site), changing the enzyme's shape so the substrate can't bind. Sketch: enzyme, inhibitor stuck on the side, active site warped, substrate not fitting.

questions.q: What is allosteric activation?
questions.a: An activator binds the allosteric site and changes the enzyme's shape so it binds substrate more efficiently.

questions.q: What is feedback inhibition? Which enzyme does the product block on the slide?
questions.a: The product of a pathway inhibits an enzyme in that pathway, slowing or stopping more product. It blocks enzyme 1 (at its allosteric site).

questions.q: How are enzymes regulated? (Checkpoint Q5)
questions.a: Competitive inhibitors, allosteric inhibitors, allosteric activators, feedback inhibition (plus temperature and pH).

questions.q: Most common source of coenzymes?
questions.a: Dietary vitamins.

questions.q: Relationship between enzymes and thermodynamics? (Checkpoint Q6)
questions.a: Enzymes lower activation energy so reactions go faster, but they don't change ΔG, so they can't make an endergonic reaction spontaneous. They aren't used up.

questions.q: How can you see catalase working? Write the equation.
questions.a: Bubbling oxygen. 2H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> → 2H<sub>2</sub>O + O<sub>2</sub>

questions.q: Two ways to measure amylase activity?
questions.a: Measure the maltose produced from starch, or use iodine to test whether starch is still present.

questions.q: Two ways to measure the speed of an enzyme reaction?
questions.a: Measure how much product is made (oxygen), or how much substrate (H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>) is left when you stop it.

questions.q: Why does the oxygen-produced graph level off?
questions.a: The substrate (hydrogen peroxide) got used up.

questions.q: Yeast-lactose experiment: purpose of the balloons, what goes in the control, IV and DV?
questions.a: Balloons catch CO<sub>2</sub> (shows how much sugar the yeast used). Control: yeast + water, no sugar. IV: type of sugar (and lactase added or not). DV: CO<sub>2</sub> produced (balloon size).

questions.q: Yeasts are what kind of organism, and what do they produce from sugar?
questions.a: Single-celled fungi, heterotrophs. CO<sub>2</sub>.

questions.q: Essential questions: what allows milk digestion, and why can some adults still do it?
questions.a: Lactase hydrolyzes lactose into glucose and galactose in the small intestine. Lactase-persistent adults keep making lactase after infancy.

questions.q: What happens in a lactose-intolerant person's gut?
questions.a: Lactose isn't broken down, reaches the large intestine, and bacteria ferment it into gas and acids: diarrhea, pain, gas, bloating.

questions.q: List the levels of organization in order from smallest (atom) to largest (biosphere).
questions.a: Atom → molecule → cell → tissue → organ → organ system → organism → population → community → ecosystem → biosphere.

questions.q: In the sequence subatomic particles → atoms → molecules → cells → tissues → organs → organ systems, why is the cell the most important level?
questions.a: The cell is the smallest level that is alive. Atoms and molecules are not alive; cells are the smallest unit that can carry out all the characteristics of life.

questions.q: Name the level of organization for each: (a) one nerve cell, (b) the stomach, (c) the digestive system, (d) all the elephants in one savanna, (e) the elephants, zebras and trees in that savanna, (f) those living things plus the soil, water and air, (g) one water molecule.
questions.a: (a) cell, (b) organ, (c) organ system, (d) population, (e) community, (f) ecosystem, (g) molecule.

questions.q: What is the difference between a population and a community? Between a community and an ecosystem?
questions.a: Population = one species in an area. Community = all the different populations (species) living together in an area. Ecosystem = the community plus the nonliving physical environment (water, soil, air).

questions.q: What is an emergent property? Explain it using minnows: what does one minnow do in a tank vs a group of minnows?
questions.a: A new property that shows up at a higher level of organization that the parts don't have on their own. One minnow in a tank swims aimlessly. A group of minnows schools together, stays in the dark patches and avoids the light. Schooling only exists at the group level.

questions.q: Apply: Give your own example of an emergent property at a different level of organization.
questions.a: Any example where the whole can do something the parts can't. Examples: one heart muscle cell can't pump blood but the heart (organ) can; a single amino acid has no function but a folded protein (enzyme) does; one bee can't run a hive but the colony can.

questions.q: A donor heart is kept beating in a machine outside the body. Is this heart alive? Answer using levels of organization and the characteristics of life.
questions.a: The heart is an organ made of living cells, and those cells are alive (they process energy and respond). But the heart by itself is not a living organism: it can't reproduce, can't maintain its own homeostasis without the machine, and depends on the rest of the organ systems. Its cells are alive; the heart alone isn't an organism.

questions.q: Name the three domains and the six kingdoms. Sort the six kingdoms into their domains.
questions.a: Domains: Bacteria, Archaea, Eukarya. Kingdoms: Eubacteria (Bacteria), Archaebacteria (Archaea), and Protista, Plantae, Fungi, Animalia (all Eukarya).

questions.q: What is LUCA? Who defined the Archaea, when, and what technique did he use?
questions.a: LUCA = last universal common ancestor, the root of the tree of life. Carl Woese defined the Archaea in 1977 using phylogenetic taxonomy of 16S ribosomal RNA.

questions.q: Apply: On the six kingdoms / three domains tree, which kingdom is Fungi most closely related to? How can you tell from the tree?
questions.a: Animalia. Fungi and Animalia branch off from the same point (they share the most recent common branch), before Plantae joins.

questions.q: List the 7 levels of taxonomy in order with the memory trick. Then give the full classification of the leopard (Panthera pardus) at every level.
questions.a: Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species ("King Philip Came Over For Great Soup"). Leopard: Animalia, Chordata, Mammalia, Carnivora, Felidae, Panthera, Panthera pardus.

questions.q: Apply: Two animals are in the same family. Which other levels must they share? Must they share a genus? Which level is the most specific?
questions.a: They must share order, class, phylum and kingdom (everything above family). They don't have to share a genus. Species is the most specific level.

questions.q: In the kingdoms Plantae and Fungi, which taxonomic level replaces "phylum"?
questions.a: Division.

questions.q: What is the smallest unit of matter? Name its three particles, their charges, and where each is found.
questions.a: The atom. Protons (+) and neutrons (no charge) are in the nucleus. Electrons (−) orbit around the nucleus in shells (orbitals).

questions.q: Define atomic number and atomic mass. On the periodic table, oxygen's box shows 8, O, Oxygen and 15.999. What do the 8 and the 15.999 stand for?
questions.a: Atomic number = number of protons. Atomic mass = number of protons + neutrons. 8 = atomic number; 15.999 = atomic mass. (O is the chemical symbol, Oxygen is the element name.)

questions.q: Apply: Carbon has atomic number 6 and mass 12. Nitrogen has atomic number 7 and mass 14. For a neutral atom of each, give the number of protons, neutrons and electrons.
questions.a: Carbon: 6 protons, 6 neutrons (12 − 6), 6 electrons. Nitrogen: 7 protons, 7 neutrons (14 − 7), 7 electrons. (Neutral atom: electrons = protons.)

questions.q: Describe a Bohr model of oxygen (atomic number 8, mass 16): what is in the nucleus, and how many electrons are in each shell?
questions.a: Nucleus: 8 protons and 8 neutrons. Inner shell: 2 electrons. Outer shell: 6 electrons.

questions.q: What is an isotope? Compare carbon-12 and carbon-14 (protons and neutrons). In the notation for C-12, what are A and Z?
questions.a: An isotope is a form of the same element with the same number of protons but a different number of neutrons. C-12: 6 protons, 6 neutrons. C-14: 6 protons, 8 neutrons. A = mass number (protons + neutrons, the 12); Z = atomic number (protons, the 6).

questions.q: Give three uses of radioisotopes.
questions.a: PET (positron emission tomography) scans to diagnose disease; radiation therapy to treat certain cancers; carbon-14 decay for carbon dating. (PET and radiation therapy are part of nuclear medicine.)

questions.q: What is the maximum number of electrons in the inner shell? In outer shells? Which electrons interact with other atoms, and what two things can they do?
questions.a: Inner shell: max 2. Outer shells: max 8. The outer shell electrons interact with other atoms. They can be shared (covalent) or donated/transferred (ionic).

questions.q: Apply: Oxygen has 6 outer electrons. How many more does it need to fill its outer shell, and how does it get them when it forms water?
questions.a: It needs 2 more. It shares one electron pair with each of 2 hydrogen atoms (2 covalent bonds), making H2O.

questions.q: What is the difference between a covalent bond and an ionic bond?
questions.a: Covalent bond: electrons are shared between atoms. Ionic bond: electrons are transferred from one atom to another, making charged ions that attract.

questions.q: Apply: Classify each as nonpolar covalent, polar covalent, or ionic: (a) O2, (b) H2O, (c) NaCl, (d) CH4, (e) Cl2.
questions.a: (a) nonpolar covalent (a double bond), (b) polar covalent, (c) ionic, (d) nonpolar covalent, (e) nonpolar covalent (two identical atoms share equally).

questions.q: What makes a covalent bond polar instead of nonpolar? Why is water polar?
questions.a: In a polar covalent bond the electrons are shared unequally, so one end is slightly negative and the other slightly positive. In water, oxygen pulls the shared electrons closer, so the O side is slightly negative (δ−) and the H side is slightly positive (δ+). In a nonpolar bond (O2, CH4) sharing is even.

questions.q: What happens to the electrons when sodium and chlorine form NaCl? What is the charge on each ion afterward?
questions.a: Sodium transfers (gives) 1 electron to chlorine. Sodium becomes Na+ and chlorine becomes Cl−. The opposite charges attract: an ionic bond.

questions.q: What does a single line vs a double line mean in a structure drawing? Give an example of a molecule with a double bond.
questions.a: Single line = single bond (one shared pair). Double line = double bond (two shared pairs). O2 has a double bond (nonpolar covalent double bond).

questions.q: What is the difference between the covalent bonds inside a water molecule and the hydrogen bonds between water molecules?
questions.a: Covalent bonds hold the H's to the O inside one water molecule (shared electrons, strong). Hydrogen bonds are weak attractions between the δ+ H of one water molecule and the δ− O of a neighboring water molecule.

questions.q: List the 7 properties (characteristics) of life.
questions.a: Order, response to stimuli, reproduction, growth and development, regulation, homeostasis, energy processing.

questions.q: What does "order" mean as a property of life? Write the sequence of order from subatomic particles up to organ systems.
questions.a: Living things are highly organized. Subatomic particles → atoms → molecules → cells → tissues → organs → organ systems.

questions.q: What is the difference between a positive and a negative response to a stimulus? Define chemotaxis, phototaxis and geotaxis. What does the "tickle me plant" do?
questions.a: Positive = moving toward the stimulus; negative = moving away. Chemotaxis = response to chemicals. Phototaxis = response to light. Geotaxis = response to gravity. The tickle me plant (mimosa) folds its leaves when touched.

questions.q: Apply: Name the type of taxis and say positive or negative: (a) a moth flies toward a porch light, (b) cockroaches run away when the kitchen light turns on, (c) bacteria swim toward sugar, (d) a worm burrows down into the soil.
questions.a: (a) positive phototaxis, (b) negative phototaxis, (c) positive chemotaxis, (d) positive geotaxis (toward gravity).

questions.q: Compare asexual and sexual reproduction. What is binary fission? What kind of reproduction is a strawberry plant making a clone with a runner? What do ALL types of reproduction have in common?
questions.a: Asexual: one parent, offspring are identical copies. Sexual: two parents, offspring are a mix. Binary fission: one cell splits into two identical cells (asexual). The strawberry runner is asexual. All types pass DNA to the next generation.

questions.q: Define regulation and homeostasis. What does the word homeostasis literally mean?
questions.a: Regulation: internal functions are coordinated within systems (groups of organs working together). Homeostasis: maintaining a stable internal environment (dynamic equilibrium). Homeo = same, stasis = state.

questions.q: Define growth and development, and give one example.
questions.a:
Growth = getting bigger (more or larger cells). Development = changes an organism goes through during its life following instructions in its DNA. Example: a seed growing into a tree, a tadpole becoming a frog, a baby becoming an adult.

Note: The slide only has the title for this one, so the answer is the standard definition.

questions.q: Define autotroph and heterotroph with an example of each. Apply: classify a sunflower, a chimp, yeast, a mushroom and algae.
questions.a: Autotroph: makes its own food (from sunlight), e.g. the sunflower. Heterotroph: has to eat other things for energy, e.g. the chimp. Sunflower = autotroph, chimp = heterotroph, yeast = heterotroph, mushroom = heterotroph (fungus), algae = autotroph.

questions.q: Apply: Which characteristic of life does each show?
