(a) a lizard basking on a hot rock, (b) a marathon runner sweating, (c) a strawberry plant sending out runners, (d) a mimosa leaf folding when touched, (e) a chimp eating fruit, (f) an acorn becoming an oak, (g) your digestive organs working together.
questions.a: (a) homeostasis (thermoregulation), (b) homeostasis, (c) reproduction (asexual), (d) response to stimuli, (e) energy processing, (f) growth and development, (g) regulation.

questions.q: Apply: Fire grows, uses energy (fuel and oxygen), and "reproduces" by spreading. Explain why fire is NOT alive using at least two characteristics of life.
questions.a: Fire has no cells and no order (it isn't organized atoms → molecules → cells). It has no DNA to pass on, so it doesn't truly reproduce. It can't maintain homeostasis or regulate itself, and it doesn't respond to stimuli. It fails the characteristics even though it looks like it grows and uses energy.

questions.q: Homeostasis means maintaining a dynamic equilibrium. What does "dynamic" mean here? Give four things the body keeps in homeostasis.
questions.a: Dynamic means the body is constantly adjusting to changes in the environment; it's not a fixed state. Examples: temperature, blood sugar, threats, food availability.

questions.q: What does ghrelin do? What does leptin do and when is it released?
questions.a: Ghrelin is a hormone that makes you feel hungry. Leptin suppresses appetite. It's released after you eat a meal and signals your brain that you're not hungry.

questions.q: Put the low blood temperature feedback loop in order: brain; adrenal gland; hormone released; low blood temperature; cells increase metabolism and make more heat; messages sent. Is it positive or negative feedback?
questions.a: Low blood temperature → message → brain → message → adrenal gland → hormone → cells increase metabolism and make more heat → feedback (temperature back up). Negative feedback.

questions.q: Define negative feedback and positive feedback. Give one example of each.
questions.a: Negative feedback reverses a change to keep levels at a set point (example: blood glucose and insulin). Positive feedback keeps going in the same direction as the stimulus and speeds up the response (example: childbirth and oxytocin).

questions.q: Describe the 4 steps of the blood glucose negative feedback loop, starting when you eat a slice of pizza.
questions.a: (1) Food is digested and blood glucose rises. (2) The pancreas secretes insulin into the blood. (3) Glucose moves into cells and the liver stores it as glycogen, so blood glucose drops. (4) With lower glucose, the pancreas stops secreting insulin. It keeps glucose near a set point.

questions.q: Describe the steps of the childbirth positive feedback loop. What makes it positive feedback?
questions.a: The baby pushes on the cervix and stretches it → nerve impulses go to the brain → the brain stimulates the pituitary to release oxytocin → oxytocin makes the uterus contract, pushing the baby harder → more stretching. It's positive because it keeps going in the same direction and speeds up until the baby is born.

questions.q: Apply: Positive or negative feedback? (a) shivering when you're cold, (b) sweating when you're hot, (c) contractions getting stronger during labor, (d) insulin released after a meal.
questions.a: (a) negative, (b) negative, (c) positive, (d) negative.

questions.q: (1) What is the relationship between energy and homeostasis? (2) What happens if homeostasis is not maintained? (3) What does this have to do with entropy?
questions.a: (1) Maintaining homeostasis takes energy: the body has to spend energy (from food, as ATP) to regulate temperature, blood sugar, etc. (2) Cells and organs can't work properly; the organism gets sick and can die. (3) Living things are highly ordered (low entropy), and entropy naturally increases. Organisms have to keep taking in energy to stay ordered and stable against that.

questions.q: Define endotherm and ectotherm and give an example of each. Apply: Why does a lizard bask in the sun? Which one needs to eat more food for its size, and why?
questions.a: Endotherm: keeps a constant internal temperature (penguins). Ectotherm: outside temperature determines its internal temperature (lizard). The lizard basks to warm its body up. The endotherm needs more food, because it burns energy (metabolism) to make its own heat.

questions.q: State the central dogma of biology. Name the process for each step.
questions.a: DNA → RNA → protein. DNA → RNA is transcription. RNA → protein is translation.

questions.q: Apply: Explain how changing ONE base in DNA can change a whole protein. Use sickle cell as your example.
questions.a: The DNA base change changes the mRNA codon, which can code for a different amino acid. That changes the protein's primary structure. Since the sequence determines how it folds, the shape and function change. In sickle cell, one amino acid in hemoglobin's beta chain changes (glutamic acid → valine), so hemoglobin forms long fibers and red blood cells bend into a sickle shape.

questions.q: What is a codon? Why does RNA use U where DNA uses T?
questions.a: A codon is a set of three bases (on mRNA) that codes for one amino acid. RNA uses the base uracil instead of thymine; U pairs with A.

questions.q: Why is water a polar molecule? Which part is slightly positive and which is slightly negative?
questions.a: Electrons are shared unequally in its covalent bonds, giving it charged ends. The oxygen side is slightly negative; the hydrogen side is slightly positive.

questions.q: Why don't oil and water mix? What word describes oil?
questions.a: Oil is nonpolar (hydrophobic), so it can't form hydrogen bonds with water. Water molecules stick to each other instead and push the oil out. (Same reason lipids are hydrophobic.)

questions.q: Why does ice float? Explain using hydrogen bonds and density.
questions.a: Ice is less dense than liquid water. In ice, the hydrogen bonds are stable and lock the molecules into an open lattice that keeps them spread apart. In liquid water, hydrogen bonds constantly break and re-form, so molecules pack closer together (denser). Less dense ice floats.

questions.q: Apply: What happens to fish when lakes freeze? Why is ice floating crucial for life?
questions.a: Ice floats and forms a layer on top that insulates the water below, so the water underneath stays liquid and the fish survive. If ice sank, lakes would freeze from the bottom up and everything would freeze solid.

questions.q: What does it mean that water has a high heat capacity? Why is it important for living things? How is a Calorie defined in terms of water?
questions.a:
Water's temperature rises and falls slowly; it takes a lot of heat to warm it up and a long time to cool down. This keeps body temperature and environments (lakes, oceans) stable, which helps homeostasis. Calorie (slide): the heat energy needed to raise 1 gram of water 1°C.

Note: Heads up: the slide calls that a "Calorie" with a capital C. Technically, 1 g of water by 1°C is a lowercase calorie; the food Calorie is 1,000 of those. Use whatever your teacher uses.

questions.q: Apply: A coastal city and an inland city are at the same latitude. Which one has smaller temperature swings between summer and winter, and why?
questions.a: The coastal city. The ocean water has a high heat capacity, so it heats and cools slowly and keeps nearby air temperatures more stable.

questions.q: What does high heat of vaporization mean, and what causes it? Apply: Explain why sweating cools you off.
questions.a: It takes a lot of heat to turn liquid water into gas, because the hydrogen bonds between water molecules have to be broken. Water doesn't evaporate easily. When sweat evaporates, it takes a lot of heat away from your skin with it, cooling you down (homeostasis).

questions.q: Why is water called a solvent? What is dissociation? Why is this important for life?
questions.a: Water dissolves a huge number of solutes (because it's polar) and can change their properties. Dissociation = atoms break off from molecules and form ions (NaCl → Na+ and Cl−). It matters because cells need dissolved substances (ions, sugars, nutrients) to move around and react; reactions in cells happen in water.

questions.q: When salt dissolves, which end of a water molecule faces the Na+ ion and which faces the Cl− ion? Why?
questions.a: The oxygen end (δ−) faces Na+. The hydrogen ends (δ+) face Cl−. Opposite charges attract.

questions.q: Define cohesion, adhesion and surface tension. What causes all three? What insect uses surface tension to walk on water?
questions.a: Cohesion = water sticks to itself. Adhesion = water sticks to other (polar or charged) things. Surface tension = water's surface acts like a skin. All caused by hydrogen bonds. The water strider walks on water.

questions.q: Apply: How does water get from the soil to the leaves of a plant? Use cohesion and adhesion.
questions.a: Adhesion: water sticks to the walls of the thin tubes in the plant and climbs them. Cohesion: water molecules are hydrogen bonded to each other, so as water evaporates from the leaves it pulls the chain of water molecules behind it up from the roots.

questions.q: Water dissociates into which two ions? Give the names and formulas.
questions.a: Hydrogen ions (H+, which join water to make hydronium, H3O+) and hydroxide ions (OH−).

questions.q: What does an acid add to water? A base? Name one example acid and one example base. In acids, which is greater, [H+] or [OH−]?
questions.a: An acid adds H+ ions (hydrochloric acid, HCl). A base adds OH− ions (sodium hydroxide, NaOH). In an acid, [H+] > [OH−]; in a base, [H+] < [OH−]; neutral = equal.

questions.q: How do you neutralize an acid? What do you do if you get acid on your skin?
questions.a:
Add a base (it cancels out the H+ with OH−). For an acid burn, flush the area with lots of cool running water to dilute and wash it away.

Note: The slide only asks these; the answers are standard lab safety.

questions.q: Apply (connects to enzymes): Pepsin works in the stomach (pH about 2). What would likely happen to pepsin if it were moved to a solution at pH 8? Why?
questions.a: It would slow down or stop working. Each enzyme has an optimum pH; pepsin's is acidic. At pH 8 its shape (active site) changes and it can denature, so it can't bind its substrate.

questions.q: What about the carbon atom makes it ideal for life? Include its electrons, the number of bonds it makes, and what shapes it can form. What does "organic" mean?
questions.a: Carbon has 6 protons and 6 electrons, with 4 electrons in its outer shell. It needs 4 more, so it forms 4 covalent bonds. That lets it build long chains, branches and rings, a stable backbone for big molecules. Organic = contains carbon bonded to hydrogen.

questions.q: Apply: Hydrogen can only form 1 bond. Why couldn't hydrogen be the backbone of macromolecules like carbon is?
questions.a: With only 1 bond, a hydrogen atom can only cap the end of a chain. It can't connect to two or more atoms, so it can't build chains, branches or rings. Carbon's 4 bonds let it connect in many directions.

questions.q: Define monomer and polymer. What pattern do ALL biological macromolecules follow?
questions.a: Monomer = single unit. Polymer = many units bound together. All are built as monomer + monomer + monomer... joined into a polymer.

questions.q: When two glucose molecules join by dehydration synthesis, where do the atoms of the water come from, which side of the equation is the water on, and what bond forms?
questions.a: An OH from one glucose and an H from the other combine into H2O, which is a product (right side). The rings join through an O bridge: a glycosidic (covalent) bond.

questions.q: Apply: (a) What is the bond called when dehydration synthesis joins two monosaccharides? Two amino acids? (b) How many water molecules are released making: a triglyceride, a 10 amino acid polypeptide, a 5-glucose chain?
questions.a: (a) Glycosidic bond; peptide bond. (b) Triglyceride: 3 (one per fatty acid). 10 amino acids: 9. 5 glucose: 4. (Chain of n monomers = n − 1 waters.)

questions.q: Apply: Dehydration synthesis or hydrolysis? (a) lactase breaking lactose, (b) building a protein, (c) cellulase breaking cellulose in a cow's gut, (d) making a triglyceride, (e) ATP → ADP + energy.
questions.a: (a) hydrolysis, (b) dehydration synthesis, (c) hydrolysis, (d) dehydration synthesis, (e) hydrolysis.

questions.q: What speeds up both reactions? Connect: Which reaction is anabolic and which is catabolic?
questions.a: Enzymes (a specific enzyme for each macromolecule). Dehydration synthesis builds = anabolic. Hydrolysis breaks down = catabolic.

questions.q: A classmate says "hydrolysis builds molecules because water is added." Correct them.
questions.a: Wrong. Hydrolysis adds water to BREAK a polymer into monomers ("split with water"). Dehydration synthesis is the one that builds, and it removes water.

questions.q: Ratio of C:H:O in carbohydrates and the general formula? Apply: A molecule is C5H10O5. Is it a carbohydrate? Pentose or hexose? Example?
questions.a: 1:2:1, (CH2O)n. Yes, it fits 1:2:1. It has 5 carbons, so it's a pentose, like ribose.

questions.q: Formula of glucose? What is an isomer? Name glucose's two isomers.
questions.a: C6H12O6. Isomers have the same chemical formula but a different structure. Fructose and galactose.

questions.q: What monosaccharides make lactose? Sucrose? Which is table sugar, which is milk sugar, and which is the most common disaccharide?
questions.a: Lactose = glucose + galactose (milk sugar). Sucrose = glucose + fructose (table sugar, the most common disaccharide).

questions.q: Classify each as a monosaccharide, disaccharide or polysaccharide: glucose, starch, lactose, fructose, glycogen, sucrose, cellulose, galactose, chitin.
questions.a: Mono: glucose, fructose, galactose. Di: lactose, sucrose. Poly: starch, glycogen, cellulose, chitin.

questions.q: Looking at a structural drawing, how can you tell if a carbohydrate is a monosaccharide, disaccharide or polysaccharide?
questions.a: Count the sugar rings. One ring = monosaccharide. Two rings joined by an O bridge = disaccharide. Many repeating rings = polysaccharide (like amylose/starch).

questions.q: Fill in: energy storage carb in plants ___ and in animals ___; structural carb in plants ___ and in animals ___. Where is glycogen stored?
questions.a: Storage: starch (plants), glycogen (animals). Structure: cellulose (plant cell walls), chitin (exoskeletons). Glycogen is stored in the liver and muscles.

questions.q: Why is starch found in seeds? What enzyme starts breaking starch down in your mouth, and into what?
questions.a: Starch is stored food for the embryo when the seed germinates. Amylase (in saliva) breaks it into smaller sugars like maltose and glucose.

questions.q: A cicada sheds its old exoskeleton (cuticle). What is it made of, and what class of macromolecule is that? What are plant cell walls made of?
questions.a: Chitin, a polysaccharide (carbohydrate). Plant cell walls are made of cellulose (also a polysaccharide).

questions.q: Apply: A runner eats a big pasta dinner (starch) the night before a race. Trace what happens to the starch from mouth to muscle.
questions.a: Amylase in saliva starts breaking starch down by hydrolysis into smaller sugars; it ends up as glucose that's absorbed into the blood. The liver and muscles take up glucose and store it as glycogen. During the race, muscles break glycogen back into glucose and use it (glycolysis) for energy.

questions.q: What do nonpolar and hydrophobic mean? Why are lipids nonpolar?
questions.a: Nonpolar = no charged ends. Hydrophobic = water fearing, doesn't dissolve in water. Lipids are mostly C–C and C–H bonds, which share electrons evenly.

questions.q: List 5 functions of lipids and name the type of lipid that does each one.
questions.a: Long-term energy storage (fats), insulation (fats), covering/waterproofing and protection (waxes), cell membrane structure (phospholipids, cholesterol), hormones (steroids like estrogen and testosterone).

questions.q: Describe the structure of a triglyceride. How many water molecules are released when one forms?
questions.a: 1 glycerol (3-carbon backbone) with 3 fatty acid tails attached, one on each carbon. 3 water molecules are released.

questions.q: Why is a triglyceride technically not a polymer? (Think about dehydration synthesis of a fat.)
questions.a: A polymer is a long chain of repeating monomers. A triglyceride is just 1 glycerol + 3 fatty acids joined by dehydration synthesis (3 waters released). It doesn't repeat and can't keep growing.

questions.q: Compare saturated and unsaturated fats: bonds, shape, room-temperature state, and one example each.
questions.a: Saturated: only single bonds, max hydrogens, straight, solid (butter, lard; palmitic or stearic acid). Unsaturated: one or more double bonds, kinked, liquid (vegetable/olive oil; linoleic or oleic acid).

questions.q: Why have many places banned trans fats? Where do trans fats come from?
questions.a: They raise LDL ("bad" cholesterol), which builds plaque in arteries and leads to heart disease. They're made by artificially hydrogenating oils (margarine, shortening, some fried and processed food).

questions.q: Why are aquatic birds' feathers and leaf surfaces covered in wax?
questions.a: Wax is hydrophobic, so it keeps water off (waterproofing) and protects them.

questions.q: Name the parts of a phospholipid and say which part is hydrophilic and which is hydrophobic. How is it different from a triglyceride?
questions.a: Head: phosphate group + glycerol (hydrophilic). Two fatty acid tails (hydrophobic). A triglyceride has 3 fatty acids and no phosphate group.

questions.q: Describe how phospholipids are arranged in the cell membrane, and where cholesterol sits.
questions.a: Two layers (a bilayer). The hydrophilic heads face the water on the inside and outside of the cell; the hydrophobic tails point toward each other in the middle. Cholesterol is tucked between the phospholipids inside the bilayer.

questions.q: What does amphipathic mean? What is the main component of the cell membrane, and what about that molecule is significant?
questions.a: Amphipathic = has a hydrophilic part and a hydrophobic part. The main component is the phospholipid. Its heads love water and its tails avoid it, so phospholipids line up in a bilayer: heads facing the water inside and outside the cell, tails hidden in the middle. That forms the barrier around the cell.

questions.q: Why are steroids grouped with lipids? How are they different from other lipids? Give three examples.
questions.a: They're hydrophobic / insoluble in water like other lipids. They're different because they're built of 4 fused carbon rings, not fatty acid chains on glycerol. Examples: cholesterol, estrogen, testosterone.

questions.q: What does cholesterol do in the cell membrane? Name the three things it lets animal cells do.
questions.a: It's an essential part of animal cell membranes that keeps the membrane's integrity and fluidity. It lets animal cells (a) not need a cell wall, (b) change shape, (c) move freely.

questions.q: Apply: Identify each lipid: (a) 4 fused rings, doesn't dissolve in water, (b) glycerol + 2 fatty acids + a phosphate group, (c) glycerol + 3 straight fatty acid chains, solid at room temp, (d) long hydrophobic coating on a leaf, (e) glycerol + 3 kinked chains, liquid at room temp.
questions.a: (a) steroid, (b) phospholipid, (c) saturated fat (triglyceride), (d) wax, (e) unsaturated fat / oil (triglyceride).

questions.q: List 6 functions of proteins and give an example protein for each.
questions.a: Support/structure: keratin. Enzymes: lactase, amylase. Transport: hemoglobin. Defense: immunoglobulins (antibodies). Hormones: insulin. Motion: actin and myosin (muscle). (Myoglobin stores oxygen in muscle.)

questions.q: Give 5 examples of proteins. What are the spikes on the coronavirus made of?
questions.a: Lactase, hemoglobin, insulin, keratin, myoglobin. The spikes are proteins.

questions.q: Name the four things attached to the central carbon of every amino acid.
questions.a: An amine group (NH2), a carboxyl group (COOH), a hydrogen (H), and an R group (side chain).

questions.q: What do all amino acids have in common? What differs between them, and what does that part determine? How many amino acids are there?
questions.a: All have an amine group (NH2), a carboxyl group (COOH) and an H on the central carbon. They differ in the R group (side chain), which determines their chemical and physical properties (polarity, acidity). There are 20.

questions.q: What is an essential amino acid? Give an example. What makes an amino acid aromatic? Name two.
questions.a: Essential = the body can't make it, so you have to get it from your diet (tryptophan). Aromatic = has a ring in its R group (tryptophan, phenylalanine; histidine on the guided learning).

questions.q: Valine's R group is CH<sub>3</sub>–CH–CH<sub>3</sub>. Serine's R group is HO–CH<sub>2</sub>. Which one is hydrophilic, and why?
questions.a: Serine. Its R group has a hydroxyl (OH), which is polar and can make hydrogen bonds with water. Valine's R group is nonpolar.

questions.q: Which element in methionine's side chain gives it its unique properties? Why that one and not carbon?
questions.a: Sulfur. Every amino acid has carbon; the S is what's unusual about methionine's R group.

questions.q: Leucine, isoleucine and phenylalanine: which one is least like the others, and why?
questions.a: Phenylalanine. Its R group is a ring (aromatic); leucine and isoleucine have branched carbon chains.

questions.q: When two amino acids join, where does the water come from? Between which two atoms is the peptide bond? What are the N terminal and C terminal?
questions.a: The OH comes from the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the H from the amine group of the other. The peptide bond is between the C (of the C=O) and the N. N terminal = the end with the free amine group; C terminal = the end with the free carboxyl group.

questions.q: Apply: (a) How many peptide bonds and waters to make a tripeptide? (b) A 50 amino acid polypeptide? (c) Bradykinin has 9 amino acids; how many peptide bonds? (d) A chain has 12 peptide bonds; how many amino acids?
questions.a: (a) 2 and 2. (b) 49 and 49. (c) 8. (d) 13. (n amino acids = n − 1 peptide bonds.)

questions.q: A polypeptide is written H2N–CH(R1)–CO–NH–CH(R2)–CO–NH–CH(R3)–CO–NH–CH(R4)–COOH. How many amino acids and how many peptide bonds does it have? How do you spot where one amino acid ends and the next begins?
questions.a: 4 amino acids, 3 peptide bonds. Each amino acid is one repeating N–C–C unit with its own R group; they're joined at the peptide bonds (the CO–NH links).

questions.q: Myoglobin's amino acid sequence starts M G L S. Name those amino acids. What level of structure is a sequence like this, and how many amino acids are in myoglobin?
questions.a: Methionine, glycine, leucine, serine. Primary structure. 154.

questions.q: For each level of protein structure (primary, secondary, tertiary, quaternary), say what it is AND what bonds or interactions hold it together.
questions.a: Primary: sequence of amino acids; covalent peptide bonds. Secondary: local folding into alpha helices and beta pleated sheets; hydrogen bonds between backbone C=O and N–H. Tertiary: overall 3D shape of one chain; R group interactions (hydrophobic interactions, hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, disulfide bonds). Quaternary: two or more polypeptide chains together; interactions between the chains (hydrophobic, hydrogen bonds, ionic).

questions.q: What are the two kinds of secondary structure? What type of bond holds them, and between which backbone atoms?
questions.a: Alpha helix (a coil) and beta pleated sheet (folds lying side by side). Hydrogen bonds between the C=O of one part of the backbone and the N–H of another.

questions.q: Name the 4 interactions that hold a protein's tertiary structure together and describe each in a few words.
questions.a: Hydrophobic interactions: nonpolar R groups tuck into the center away from water. Hydrophilic interactions / hydrogen bonds: polar R groups face outward toward water. Ionic bonds: oppositely charged R groups attract. Disulfide bonds: covalent bonds between the S atoms of two cysteines.

questions.q: Which tertiary interaction is the only covalent one? Where do hydrophobic R groups end up in a folded protein, and why?
questions.a: The disulfide bond (between the S atoms of two cysteines). Hydrophobic R groups tuck into the center to avoid water; hydrophilic ones face outward toward water.

questions.q: Compare myoglobin and hemoglobin: how they're alike, number of chains, number of hemes, level of structure, and job.
questions.a: Alike: both are proteins with alpha helices and iron-containing heme groups that bind oxygen. Myoglobin: 1 chain, 1 heme, tertiary, stores O2 in muscle. Hemoglobin: 4 chains, 4 hemes, quaternary, carries O2 in blood.

questions.q: Sickle cell disease: which protein, which chain, what change, and what does that change do to the hemoglobin and the red blood cells?
questions.a: Hemoglobin, the beta chain. One amino acid is swapped (glutamic acid → valine). The hemoglobin forms long fibers, which bend red blood cells into a sickle shape.

questions.q: What is denaturation? What three things cause it? Does the primary structure change? Why does losing shape matter so much for an enzyme?
questions.a: The protein loses its shape and therefore its function. Caused by heat, pH changes, and chemicals. The primary structure (sequence) does NOT change. An enzyme binds its specific substrate at its active site, so if the shape changes, the substrate can't fit.

questions.q: Apply: Explain using protein structure: (a) why an egg white turns solid and white when you fry it, (b) why a very high fever is dangerous.
questions.a: (a) Heat denatures the albumin protein in the egg white; it unfolds and can't go back (irreversible). (b) High body temperature can denature your proteins and enzymes, so they lose their shape and stop working.

questions.q: What is the overall function of nucleic acids? Why are they important for the continuity of life? Give the full names of DNA and RNA.
questions.a: They store and pass on genetic information (the cell's instructions), copied from parent to offspring. Deoxyribonucleic acid and ribonucleic acid.

questions.q: What are the three parts of a nucleotide? Which parts form the backbone of a DNA strand?
questions.a: A sugar (deoxyribose or ribose), a phosphate, and a nitrogen base. The sugar and phosphate alternate to form the backbone; the bases stick off it.

questions.q: Purines vs pyrimidines: how many rings, which bases, and the memory trick.
questions.a: Purines: 2 rings, adenine and guanine ("Pure As Gold"). Pyrimidines: 1 ring, cytosine, thymine and uracil ("CUT").

questions.q: One DNA strand reads 5′ A T G C 3′. Write the other strand and label its 5′ and 3′ ends. Which bases in your answer are purines?
questions.a: 3′ T A C G 5′ (it runs the opposite way: antiparallel). Purines are A and G (two rings).

questions.q: What does antiparallel mean?
questions.a: The two DNA strands run in opposite directions: one goes 5′ to 3′, the other 3′ to 5′. The 5′ end of one strand lines up with the 3′ end of the other.

questions.q: Apply: (a) DNA AATTGC: write the complementary DNA and the complementary RNA. (b) Same for DNA TACGGA.
questions.a: (a) DNA: TTAACG. RNA: UUAACG. (b) DNA: ATGCCT. RNA: AUGCCU.

questions.q: Compare DNA and RNA: sugar, bases, number of strands, main job, and location.
questions.a: DNA: deoxyribose, A T G C, double helix, stores genetic info, stays in the nucleus. RNA: ribose, A U G C, usually single-stranded, protein synthesis, leaves the nucleus.

questions.q: Apply: A DNA sample is 30% adenine. What percent is thymine? Guanine? Cytosine? Explain.
questions.a: Thymine 30% (A always pairs with T). That leaves 40% for G + C, so guanine 20% and cytosine 20% (G pairs with C).

questions.q: Apply: You mix starch with amylase and wait. What would iodine show compared to the start? What product could you test for to prove amylase worked?
questions.a: Iodine would no longer turn blue-black (or much less), because the starch got broken down. Amylase makes maltose, a sugar, so you could test for it (Benedict's turns positive).

questions.q: Define metabolism and bioenergetics.
questions.a: Metabolism = the sum of all chemical reactions in an organism (or cell). Bioenergetics = the study of energy flow through living systems.

questions.q: Compare catabolic and anabolic reactions: what each does, energy in or out, exergonic or endergonic, the letter equation, and the memory trick.
questions.a: Catabolic: breaks down larger molecules, releases energy, exergonic, degradation, AB → A + B + energy ("cats break things"). Anabolic: builds complex molecules, uses energy, endergonic, synthesis, A + B → AB ("Anakin built the Death Star").

questions.q: Apply: Catabolic or anabolic? (a) building a protein from amino acids, (b) digesting starch, (c) photosynthesis making glucose, (d) breaking down glucose for ATP, (e) copying DNA, (f) lactase breaking lactose.
questions.a: (a) anabolic, (b) catabolic, (c) anabolic, (d) catabolic, (e) anabolic, (f) catabolic.

questions.q: Define energy. What's the difference between kinetic and potential energy? What is chemical energy?
questions.a: Energy = the ability to do work. Kinetic = energy of motion. Potential = stored energy. Chemical energy = potential energy stored in chemical bonds.

questions.q: A cyclist rides up a hill and coasts down the other side. Where is potential energy highest? Where is kinetic energy highest? What happens on the way down?
questions.a: Potential energy is highest at the top. Kinetic energy is highest at the bottom. On the way down, potential energy turns into kinetic energy (energy out).

questions.q: State the first and second laws of thermodynamics (give two ways to state the second law).
questions.a: First law: energy can't be created or destroyed (conservation of energy), only transferred or transformed. Second law: in a closed system, entropy (randomness) tends to increase over time; also, heat flows from higher temperature to lower temperature.

questions.q: 1000 J of sunlight reaches a plant. About how much energy ends up available in the plant, the herbivore that eats it, and the carnivore that eats the herbivore? Where does the rest go?
questions.a: Plant 10 J, herbivore 1 J, carnivore 0.1 J (990 J, 9 J and 0.9 J lost). The rest is lost to the environment as heat (second law); it isn't destroyed (first law).

questions.q: Apply: If a producer stores 500 J, about how much reaches the second consumer (the carnivore that eats the herbivore)? Why does so much disappear?
questions.a: About 5 J (500 → 50 → 5, roughly 10% passes on each step). The rest is lost as heat at each transfer (second law); no transfer is 100% efficient.

questions.q: Rank solid, liquid and gas from lowest to highest entropy. Is ΔS positive or negative when ice melts into a puddle?
questions.a: Solid < liquid < gas. Ice melting: ΔS is positive (entropy increases).

questions.q: If entropy always increases, why don't living things (and systems on Earth) fall into disorder and chaos?
questions.a: They're open systems that keep taking in energy, ultimately from the sun. That constant energy input lets them stay ordered.

questions.q: What three things must organisms be able to do to follow the laws of thermodynamics? What five things do living things need energy for?
questions.a: (1) Obtain energy from their surroundings (sun, food, chemicals), (2) transform it into usable energy to do work (ATP), (3) lose some as heat during each transfer. Energy is needed for metabolism, homeostasis, movement and activity, growth and development, reproduction.

questions.q: Compare exergonic and endergonic reactions: energy, sign of ΔG, spontaneous or not, "uphill" or "downhill," and one example each.
questions.a: Exergonic: releases energy, ΔG negative, spontaneous, downhill (products lower than reactants), e.g. combustion or breaking down glucose. Endergonic: requires/absorbs energy, ΔG positive, non-spontaneous, uphill (products higher), e.g. photosynthesis or melting ice.

questions.q: On an energy graph, how do you tell an exergonic reaction from an endergonic one? Where on the graph do you measure activation energy and ΔG?
questions.a: Exergonic: products end lower than reactants (downhill). Endergonic: products end higher (uphill). Activation energy = from the reactants up to the peak of the hump. ΔG = the difference between reactants and products.

questions.q: What is activation energy? What is the transition state? What does heating a system do to reactions?
questions.a: Activation energy = the energy needed to get a reaction started. Transition state = the high-energy, unstable, contorted state right before bonds break. Heating makes reactants react faster.

questions.q: "Spontaneous means it happens fast." True or false? Explain.
questions.a: False. Spontaneous means no outside energy is needed (exergonic). It can still be slow, like iron rusting.

questions.q: Define enzyme, substrate, active site and enzyme-substrate complex.
questions.a: Enzyme: a protein that acts as an organic catalyst to speed up reactions (by lowering activation energy). Substrate: the reactant the enzyme attaches to. Active site: the spot on the enzyme where the substrate binds. Enzyme-substrate complex: the enzyme and substrate bound together.

questions.q: List four properties of enzymes.
questions.a: Made of proteins; speed up reactions; unchanged after each reaction (reusable); specific to their substrate.

questions.q: For each enzyme give what it breaks down and where: lactase, amylase, pepsin, lipase, alcohol dehydrogenase.
questions.a: Lactase: lactose (milk) to simple sugars, small intestine. Amylase: starch to simple sugars, saliva. Pepsin: proteins to amino acids, stomach. Lipase: fats to fatty acids, pancreas/intestine. Alcohol dehydrogenase: alcohol to non-toxic substances and sugar, liver/stomach.

questions.q: Apply: Using the naming rule, what would you call the enzyme that breaks down maltose? Sucrose? What ending do most enzymes have?
questions.a: Maltase. Sucrase. Most enzyme names end in -ase (named after the substrate).

questions.q: Describe the 4 steps of sucrase breaking down sucrose. What happens to the enzyme at the end?
questions.a: (1) Sucrase and sucrose are available. (2) Sucrose binds the active site, forming the enzyme-substrate complex. (3) Water is added and sucrose is split (hydrolysis). (4) Glucose and fructose are released. The enzyme comes out unchanged and can be reused.

questions.q: What is the induced fit model? How is it different from the lock and key model?
questions.a: Induced fit: substrate and enzyme fit together, and the enzyme's shape shifts slightly when the substrate binds to get the best fit. Lock and key is the older idea of a rigid, perfect fit. (Your class slide calls them the same thing; know both.)

questions.q: What is the difference between an enzyme doing degradation and an enzyme doing synthesis?
questions.a: Degradation: the enzyme breaks one substrate down into smaller products. Synthesis: the enzyme combines substrates into one larger product. The enzyme is unchanged either way.

questions.q: An energy graph shows the same reaction with and without an enzyme. What is different between the two curves, and what stays the same?
questions.a: With the enzyme, the hump (activation energy) is lower. The starting and ending energy levels stay the same, so ΔG doesn't change.

questions.q: Lactose is made of which two sugars joined by what bond? Where are the products absorbed? How many subunits does lactase have, how many amino acids total, and what level of structure is that?
questions.a: Galactose + glucose, glycosidic bond. Absorbed by cells of the small intestine. 4 subunits of 1023 amino acids each, 4092 total; quaternary structure.

questions.q: List four factors that affect enzyme speed. Give three ways to increase the rate of an enzymatic reaction. What is the optimum?
questions.a: Substrate concentration, temperature, pH, enzyme concentration. Increase rate: add more substrate, add more enzyme, move temperature or pH toward the optimum. Optimum = the temperature or pH where the enzyme reacts fastest.

questions.q: Describe the shape of an enzyme's rate vs temperature graph and rate vs pH graph. What does the peak of each represent?
questions.a: Temperature: the rate rises slowly to a peak, then drops off steeply (denaturation). pH: a bell-shaped curve around one pH. The peak is the optimum, where the enzyme works fastest.

questions.q: Why does enzyme activity drop sharply above the optimum temperature?
questions.a: The enzyme denatures: it changes shape so much (including the active site) that the substrate can't bind, so it stops working.

questions.q: Apply: Why are Siamese cats darker on their nose, ears, paws and tail? Predict what a Siamese cat raised somewhere very cold would look like.
questions.a: Their enzyme tyrosinase only works below about 33°C; it makes dark pigment. Those body parts are cooler, so the enzyme works there. A cat raised in a very cold place would be darker over more of its body.

questions.q: Compare competitive inhibition, allosteric inhibition and allosteric activation: where does the molecule bind, and what does it do to the enzyme?
questions.a: Competitive: the inhibitor binds the active site and blocks the substrate. Allosteric inhibition: the inhibitor binds a different site (allosteric site) and changes the enzyme's shape so the substrate can't bind. Allosteric activation: an activator binds the allosteric site and changes the shape so the substrate binds more efficiently.

questions.q: Explain these two analogies: (a) a guy (the enzyme) holding hands with his girlfriend (the substrate) turns to stare at another girl (a competitive inhibitor); (b) a wall outlet (the enzyme) has one charger plugged into the top socket (the substrate in the active site) and another plug in the other socket (a noncompetitive inhibitor). What does "if it fits, it sits" mean?
questions.a: (a) The enzyme gets pulled away from its substrate by the competitive inhibitor, which competes for the same spot (active site). (b) The outlet is the enzyme; the substrate plugs into the active site socket; the noncompetitive inhibitor plugs into the other socket (allosteric site). "If it fits, it sits" = a competitive inhibitor is shaped enough like the substrate to sit in the active site.

questions.q: In feedback inhibition in a 4-enzyme pathway, what molecule does the inhibiting, which enzyme does it block, and where does it bind?
questions.a: The final product inhibits enzyme 1 (the first enzyme) by binding its allosteric site, which slows or stops more product being made.

questions.q: What is feedback inhibition? What is the most common source of coenzymes?
questions.a: The product of a pathway becomes an inhibitor, slowing down or stopping more product from being made. Coenzymes mostly come from dietary vitamins.

questions.q: How can you see catalase working? Write its equation. Two ways to measure amylase activity?
questions.a: Bubbling oxygen. 2H2O2 → 2H2O + O2. Measure the maltose produced from starch, or use iodine to test whether starch is still there.

questions.q: On a graph of oxygen produced vs time for catalase breaking down hydrogen peroxide, what does the curve look like, and why does it level off?
questions.a: It rises fast at first, then flattens out. It levels off because the substrate (hydrogen peroxide) has been used up.

questions.q: What are the two ways to measure the speed of an enzyme reaction?
questions.a: (A) Measure how much product is made (oxygen). (B) Measure how much substrate (hydrogen peroxide) is left when the reaction is stopped.

questions.q: Yeast is put in 5 flasks with balloons: glucose, sucrose, lactose, lactose + lactase, and a control. (a) What goes in the control? (b) What are the IV and DV? (c) What do the balloons catch? (d) If yeast can't make lactase, which balloons inflate?
questions.a: (a) Yeast + water, no sugar. (b) IV: type of sugar (and whether lactase is added). DV: amount of CO2 (balloon size). (c) CO2. (d) Glucose, sucrose, and lactose + lactase inflate; lactose alone and the control stay flat.

questions.q: What kind of organism is yeast, how does it get energy, and why does it make bread rise?
questions.a: A single-celled fungus and a heterotroph. It consumes sugar and produces carbon dioxide; the CO2 gas makes bread rise.

questions.q: (1) What cellular mechanism allows the digestion of milk? (2) Why can some adults still do it? Then describe what happens in a lactose-intolerant person.
questions.a: (1) The enzyme lactase in the small intestine hydrolyzes lactose into glucose and galactose, which get absorbed. (2) Lactase-persistent people keep making lactase after infancy (a genetic change). Lactose intolerant: no lactase, so lactose reaches the large intestine where bacteria ferment it, making gas and acids → diarrhea, abdominal pain, gas, bloating.

questions.q: What is the relationship between enzymes and thermodynamics? How are enzymes regulated?
questions.a: Enzymes lower activation energy so reactions go faster, but they don't change ΔG; they can't make an endergonic reaction spontaneous, and they aren't used up. Regulation: competitive inhibitors, allosteric inhibitors, allosteric activators, feedback inhibition, and conditions like temperature and pH.

questions.q: Matching: write a (carbohydrate), b (lipid), c (protein) or d (nucleic acid). 1 contains adenine and thymine, 2 lactose, 3 chains of amino acids, 4 long-term energy storage, 5 cholesterol, 6 chains of fatty acids and glycerol, 7 plant cell walls.
For each of the 4 macromolecules, give its monomer (or building blocks) and one function.
questions.a: Carbohydrates: monosaccharides; energy and structure. Lipids: glycerol + fatty acids (no true monomer); long-term energy storage, membranes, hormones. Proteins: amino acids; enzymes, transport, support, defense, hormones, motion. Nucleic acids: nucleotides; store and pass on genetic information.

questions.q: Apply: Lactase is a protein made of 4 polypeptide chains. (a) What monomers is it made of and what bond joins them? (b) What level of structure is it? (c) What would happen if you heated it to 80°C, and why? (d) Is the reaction it catalyzes catabolic or anabolic, exergonic or endergonic, and is it dehydration synthesis or hydrolysis?
questions.a: (a) Amino acids joined by peptide bonds. (b) Quaternary. (c) It would denature: it loses its shape (active site), so lactose can't bind and it stops working. (d) Catabolic, exergonic, hydrolysis.

questions.q: Apply: A hiker is sweating on a hot day. Explain what's happening using: a property of water, homeostasis/feedback, and energy.
questions.a: Water's high heat of vaporization: evaporating sweat pulls a lot of heat away from the skin. This is homeostasis through negative feedback (body temperature rises above the set point → sweat → temperature drops back). Making sweat and regulating temperature costs energy (ATP from breaking down food), which is why homeostasis requires energy.

questions.q: Apply: Trace how the DNA for lactase becomes a working enzyme. Use: transcription, translation, codons, amino acids, peptide bonds, primary → quaternary structure.
questions.a: The lactase gene in DNA is transcribed into mRNA. The mRNA leaves the nucleus and is translated: each codon (3 bases) codes for one amino acid. Amino acids are joined by peptide bonds (dehydration synthesis) into a polypeptide (primary structure). It folds with hydrogen bonds into helices/sheets (secondary), folds into a 3D shape (tertiary), and 4 chains come together (quaternary) to make working lactase.

questions.q: Apply: Why does it matter for life that BOTH water is polar AND phospholipid tails are nonpolar?
questions.a: Because water is polar, nonpolar tails avoid it (hydrophobic) while the polar heads are attracted to it. That forces phospholipids into a bilayer with heads facing the water inside and outside the cell and tails hidden in the middle, which forms the cell membrane.

questions.q: Apply: Explain why your body needs a constant supply of energy, connecting ATP, entropy and at least one characteristic of life.
questions.a: Living things are highly ordered (low entropy), but entropy naturally increases and every energy transfer loses heat. To stay ordered, maintain homeostasis, grow and reproduce, cells constantly break down food (catabolic, exergonic) to make ATP, then use ATP to power energy-requiring (anabolic, endergonic) work.

questions.q: Which type of RNA carries the message from DNA out of the nucleus? Which is the smallest type of RNA?
questions.a: Messenger RNA (mRNA). The smallest is microRNA (miRNA).

questions.q: Humans can't digest cellulose but cows can. Explain.
questions.a: Cows (grazing animals) have bacteria and protists in their digestive system that make the enzyme cellulase, which breaks cellulose into glucose. Humans don't have that.

questions.q: Give three benefits of fiber in the diet.
questions.a: Keeps bowel movements regular, regulates how fast blood glucose is used, helps remove excess cholesterol. (Bonus: helps you feel full.)

questions.q: Why do you have to eat omega-3 fatty acids, and what's a good source? What cells store fat in animals?
questions.a: Your body can't make them (they're essential). Fish like salmon, trout and tuna. Fat is stored in adipocytes.

questions.q: Cytochrome c: where is it found, how many amino acids does the human version have, and what can comparing it between species tell us?
questions.a: In the mitochondria. 104 amino acids. Differences give clues about evolutionary relationships and a common ancestor (humans and chimps are identical; rhesus monkeys differ by 1).

questions.q: Where is DNA found? What is a genome? What do DNA and histones form?
questions.a: In the nucleus of eukaryotic cells (also mitochondria and chloroplasts). Genome = the cell's entire genetic content. DNA + histone proteins = chromatin.

questions.q: For each, name the indicator test and what a POSITIVE result looks like: (a) starch, (b) simple sugars, (c) protein, (d) lipids.
questions.a: (a) Iodine (Lugol's): turns blue-black. (b) Benedict's solution (heated): blue → green, yellow, orange or red. (c) Biuret: blue → purple/violet. (d) Brown paper: leaves a translucent (see-through) grease spot; or Sudan III: red layer.

questions.q: Apply: You test an unknown food. Iodine stays orange-brown, Benedict's turns orange, biuret stays blue, and it leaves a see-through spot on brown paper. Which biomolecules are present and which aren't?
questions.a: Present: simple sugar and lipid. Not present: starch and protein.

questions.q: Apply: How could you test whether lactase broke down the lactose in milk?
questions.a: Measure the glucose produced (for example with a glucose test strip) before and after adding lactase. You could also use the yeast-balloon setup: lactose + lactase should make CO2. (Benedict's isn't great here because lactose itself reacts with it.)

questions.q: Write the equation for breaking down glucose (cellular respiration). How is photosynthesis related to it?
questions.a: C6H12O6 + 6O2 → 6CO2 + 6H2O + energy. Photosynthesis is the reverse: plants use sunlight energy to turn CO2 (and water) into glucose.

questions.q: Apply: Use ΔG = ΔH − TΔS. (a) ΔH = −40 kJ, TΔS = +20 kJ. (b) ΔH = +30 kJ, TΔS = +10 kJ. Find ΔG for each and say exergonic or endergonic.
questions.a:
(a) ΔG = −40 − 20 = −60 kJ → exergonic (spontaneous). (b) ΔG = 30 − 10 = +20 kJ → endergonic (non-spontaneous).

Note: This formula is from the Ch 6 reading guide (OpenStax). Skip if you didn't cover it.

questions.q: What is ATP made of? What kind of reaction turns ATP into ADP + energy?
questions.a:
Adenosine bound to three phosphate groups. Hydrolysis (it's exergonic and releases energy).

Note: The ATP details come from the reading guide.

cards.front: What are biological macromolecules?
cards.back: Large molecules necessary for life, built from smaller organic (carbon-containing) molecules.

cards.front: Name the four classes of macromolecules.
cards.back: Carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, nucleic acids.

cards.front: Monomers combine to create ____. What's the difference between the two?
cards.back: Polymers. A monomer is a single unit; a polymer is many units bound together.

cards.front: What happens during dehydration synthesis? What bond forms?
cards.back: Two monomers join. An H from one and an OH from the other leave as H<sub>2</sub>O, and a covalent bond forms between them. It builds polymers.

cards.front: What happens during hydrolysis?
cards.back: Water is added to break a polymer into monomers. One piece gets an H, the other gets an OH. It breaks polymers.

cards.front: What can speed up dehydration synthesis and hydrolysis?
cards.back: Enzymes (specific ones for each macromolecule).

cards.front: What about the carbon atom makes it ideal for life?
cards.back: It has 4 outer electrons, so it forms 4 covalent bonds. That lets it build chains, branches and rings: a stable backbone for large molecules.

cards.front: Ratio of carbon to hydrogen to oxygen in carbohydrates?
cards.back: 1:2:1, written (CH<sub>2</sub>O)n. Carbon to hydrogen alone is 1:2.

cards.front: Most common monosaccharide? Most monosaccharide names end in what?
cards.back: Glucose. -ose.

cards.front: Chemical formula for glucose?
cards.back: C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub>

cards.front: Glucose is used during [cellular respiration / photosynthesis]. Excess glucose is stored as [protein / starch].
cards.back: Cellular respiration. Starch (in plants).

cards.front: Example of a pentose? A hexose?
cards.back: Pentose (5 C): ribose. Hexose (6 C): glucose (also fructose, galactose).

cards.front: Why are glucose and fructose considered isomers?
cards.back: Same chemical formula (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub>) but different structure (arrangement of atoms).

cards.front: For these three hexoses: (a) molecular formula of each? (b) same formula, different structure is called? (c) why "hexoses"?
cards.back: (a) All three are C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub>. (b) Isomers. (c) Each has 6 carbons.

cards.front: How are disaccharides formed? What's the bond called?
cards.back: Two monosaccharides join by dehydration synthesis (water released). The covalent bond is a glycosidic bond.

cards.front: Name two common disaccharides and their monomers. Which is most common?
cards.back: Sucrose (glucose + fructose) and lactose (glucose + galactose). Sucrose (table sugar) is the most common.

cards.front: What is a polysaccharide?
cards.back: A long chain of monosaccharides linked by glycosidic bonds.

cards.front: Starch is made from a mixture of ____ and ____.
cards.back: Amylose and amylopectin.

cards.front: Why is starch found in seeds?
cards.back: It's stored food for the embryo when the seed germinates.

cards.front: What is amylase?
cards.back: An enzyme (in saliva) that breaks starch down into smaller sugars like maltose and glucose.

cards.front: How do animals store glucose? Where?
cards.back: As glycogen, the animal equivalent of starch, stored in liver and muscle cells.

cards.front: What is a plant's cell wall made from?
cards.back: Cellulose.

cards.front: How do grazing animals break down cellulose?
cards.back: Bacteria and protists living in their digestive system secrete the enzyme cellulase, which breaks cellulose into glucose.

cards.front: What carbohydrate makes up insect and crustacean exoskeletons?
cards.back: Chitin.

cards.front: Energy storage carb in plants vs animals? Structural carb in plants vs animals?
cards.back: Storage: starch (plants), glycogen (animals). Structure: cellulose (plant cell walls), chitin (exoskeletons).

cards.front: Lipids tend to be [polar / nonpolar] and [soluble / insoluble] in water.
cards.back: Nonpolar, insoluble (hydrophobic).

cards.front: What does nonpolar mean?
cards.back: No charged or partially charged ends (mostly C–C and C–H bonds), so it doesn't interact with water. Hydrophobic.

cards.front: List the functions of lipids (at least 2 for the worksheet, all for the slide list).
cards.back: Long-term energy storage, insulation, covering/protection (waxes), cell membranes (phospholipids), hormones (steroids).

cards.front: Two main components of a fat molecule?
cards.back: Glycerol and fatty acids.

cards.front: Fatty acid with only single bonds is ____; with a double bond is ____.
cards.back: Saturated; unsaturated.

cards.front: Unsaturated fats are [solid / liquid] at room temperature. Why?
cards.back: Liquid. Double bonds kink the chains so they can't pack tightly.

cards.front: Compare saturated and unsaturated fats (bonds, shape, room temp, example).
cards.back: Saturated: single bonds only, straight, solid (butter, palmitic/stearic acid). Unsaturated: at least one double bond, kinked, liquid (oils, linoleic/oleic acid).

cards.front: What type of cells store fat in animals?
cards.back: Adipocytes.

cards.front: Examples of unsaturated fats?
cards.back: Olive oil, corn oil, canola oil, cod liver oil (vegetable oils).

cards.front: Why are trans fats banned in some places?
cards.back: They raise LDL ("bad" cholesterol), which causes plaque in arteries and heart disease. They're made by artificially hydrogenating oils.

cards.front: Where would you get omega-3 fatty acids?
cards.back: Fish: salmon, trout, tuna. (Your body can't make them.)

cards.front: Why do aquatic birds and leaves have a waxy covering?
cards.back: Wax is hydrophobic, so it keeps water off (waterproofing and protection).

cards.front: Where are phospholipids found?
cards.back: The cell (plasma) membrane. They're its main structural component.

cards.front: Why are phospholipids called amphipathic?
cards.back: They have a hydrophilic part (phosphate head) and a hydrophobic part (fatty acid tails).

cards.front: How do phospholipids arrange in the membrane, and why does that matter?
cards.back: As a bilayer: heads face the water inside and outside the cell, tails face each other in the middle away from water.

cards.front: How many carbon rings are in a steroid?
cards.back: 4 fused rings.

cards.front: Why are steroids grouped with lipids? What makes them different?
cards.back: Grouped because they're hydrophobic/insoluble in water. Different because they're built from fused rings, not fatty acid chains.

cards.front: Two examples of steroids?
cards.back: Cholesterol, testosterone, estrogen (any two).

cards.front: What does cholesterol do in the membrane, and what 3 things does it let animal cells do?
cards.back: Keeps membrane integrity and fluidity. Lets animal cells (a) not need a cell wall, (b) change shape, (c) move freely.

cards.front: Why are triglycerides technically not polymers?
cards.back: They aren't chains of repeating monomers. Dehydration synthesis just attaches 3 fatty acids to 1 glycerol (releasing 3 waters), and it stops there.

cards.front: Proteins are polymers of ____ joined by ____ bonds. Other name for proteins?
cards.back: Amino acids, peptide bonds. Polypeptides.

cards.front: List the six protein functions from the slide.
cards.back: Support, enzymes, transport, defense, hormones, motion.

cards.front: Give 5 examples of proteins from the slides.
cards.back: Lactase, hemoglobin, insulin, keratin, myoglobin (also amylase, immunoglobulins).

cards.front: Enzymes are ____ for biochemical reactions. What is a catabolic enzyme?
cards.back: Catalysts. An enzyme that breaks down its substrate.

cards.front: Match: amylase, hemoglobin, keratin, immunoglobulins to: a protect from pathogens, b structural, c digestive breaks down starch, d transport in blood.
cards.back: Amylase c, hemoglobin d, keratin b, immunoglobulins a.

cards.front: Name the protein: transports substances in blood / builds the cytoskeleton / protects from pathogens / muscle contraction.
cards.back: Hemoglobin (or albumin) / actin or tubulin / immunoglobulins / actin and myosin.

cards.front: Draw a generic amino acid. Label all four things on the central carbon.
cards.back: Central C bonded to: amine group (NH<sub>2</sub>), carboxyl group (COOH), H, and R group (side chain).

cards.front: What do all amino acids have in common, and what differs?
cards.back: All have NH<sub>2</sub>, COOH (and H on the central C). They differ in the R group, which defines each one.

cards.front: The nature of an amino acid (polarity, acidity) is determined by what?
cards.back: Its R group (side chain).

cards.front: How many amino acids are there?
Why are some amino acids "essential"? Example?
cards.back: The body can't make them, so they have to come from your diet. Tryptophan.

cards.front: Which element in methionine's side chain gives it unique properties?
cards.back: Sulfur.

cards.front: What makes an amino acid aromatic? Name two.
cards.back: A ring in its R group. Tryptophan, phenylalanine (histidine on the guided learning).

cards.front: Leucine, isoleucine, phenylalanine: which is least like the others and why?
cards.back: Phenylalanine. Its R group is a ring; the other two are branched carbon chains.

cards.front: Valine vs serine: how alike, how different, which is hydrophilic and why?
cards.back: Both have an amine and carboxyl group; their R groups differ. Serine is hydrophilic because its R group has a hydroxyl (–OH), which is polar and can hydrogen bond.

cards.front: Making a dipeptide: what reaction, and where does the water come from?
cards.back: Dehydration synthesis. OH from the carboxyl group of one amino acid + H from the amino group of the other.

cards.front: The peptide bond forms between which two atoms?
cards.back: The C of the C=O and the N.

cards.front: A tripeptide forms how many peptide bonds and waters? A 9 amino acid chain like bradykinin?
cards.back: Tripeptide: 2 and 2. Bradykinin: 8 peptide bonds (n − 1).

cards.front: The N terminal has a free ____ group; the C terminal has a free ____ group.
cards.back: Amino (NH<sub>2</sub>); carboxyl (COOH).

cards.front: What are the four levels of protein structure?
cards.back: Primary, secondary, tertiary, quaternary.

cards.front: The sequence of amino acids is the ____ structure. What bonds hold it?
cards.back: Primary. Covalent peptide bonds.

cards.front: First four amino acids of myoglobin (MGLS)?
cards.back: Methionine, glycine, leucine, serine.

cards.front: Sickle cell anemia is caused by a single change in what protein chain? What does the change make hemoglobin do?
cards.back: The beta chain of hemoglobin (glutamic acid swapped for valine). Hemoglobin forms long fibers that distort red blood cells into a sickle shape.

cards.front: The two secondary structures, and the bond that holds them?
cards.back: Alpha helix and beta pleated sheet. Hydrogen bonds between backbone C=O and N–H.

cards.front: The 3D structure of one protein chain is its ____ structure. Name the 4 bond types involved.
cards.back: Tertiary. Hydrophobic interactions, hydrogen bonds (hydrophilic interactions), ionic bonds, disulfide bonds.

cards.front: The nature of the R groups causes the protein to [fold / dismantle].
cards.back: Fold.

cards.front: Where do hydrophobic vs hydrophilic R groups end up in a folded protein?
cards.back: Hydrophobic toward the center (away from water). Hydrophilic on the outside (toward water).

cards.front: What is a disulfide bond, and between which amino acid?
cards.back: A covalent bond between the S atoms of two cysteines.

cards.front: Quaternary structures are formed from several ____. Example?
cards.back: Polypeptide chains (subunits). Hemoglobin: 4 chains.

cards.front: Myoglobin vs hemoglobin: alike and different?
cards.back: Alike: proteins with alpha helices and iron-containing heme groups that bind O<sub>2</sub>. Myoglobin: 1 chain, 1 heme, tertiary, stores O<sub>2</sub> in muscle. Hemoglobin: 4 chains, 4 hemes, quaternary, carries O<sub>2</sub> in blood.

cards.front: What happens when a protein is denatured? What can cause it?
cards.back: It loses its shape and therefore its function (sequence stays the same). Heat, pH changes, chemicals.

cards.front: Enzymes bind to a specific ____.
cards.back: Substrate (at the active site).

cards.front: Cytochrome c: where is it, how many amino acids in humans, and what can differences in it tell us?
cards.back: Mitochondria. 104. Evolutionary relationships and a common ancestor (not protein function).

cards.front: Why are nucleic acids important for the continuity of life?
cards.back: They carry the genetic blueprint/instructions for the cell and are passed from parent to offspring.

cards.front: Where is DNA found?
cards.back: Nucleus of eukaryotes (also mitochondria and chloroplasts). Not membrane-enclosed in prokaryotes.

cards.front: The cell's entire genetic content is its ____. In eukaryotes, DNA + histones form ____.
cards.back: Genome. Chromatin.

cards.front: RNA is mostly involved in what cellular process?
cards.back: Protein synthesis.

cards.front: DNA and RNA are made of what monomers? Three parts of each?
cards.back: Nucleotides. Sugar (5-carbon), phosphate, nitrogenous base.

cards.front: Four bases in DNA?
cards.back: Adenine, thymine, guanine, cytosine.

cards.front: Purines have [2/1] rings; pyrimidines have [2/1]. Which bases are which?
cards.back: Purines 2 rings: adenine, guanine. Pyrimidines 1 ring: cytosine, thymine, uracil.

cards.front: Sugar in DNA? In RNA? What's the difference?
cards.back: Deoxyribose; ribose. Ribose has an OH on the 2nd carbon; deoxyribose has an H there (one less oxygen).

cards.front: Shape of DNA? What's on the outside vs inside?
cards.back: Double helix. Sugar-phosphate backbone outside, base pairs inside.

cards.front: Base pairing rule?
cards.back: A–T (A–U in RNA) and G–C. Purine with pyrimidine, held by hydrogen bonds.

cards.front: What does antiparallel mean?
cards.back: The two DNA strands run in opposite directions: one 5′ to 3′, the other 3′ to 5′.

cards.front: DNA = A A T T G C. Complementary RNA?
cards.back: U U A A C G

cards.front: A set of three bases is called a ____.
cards.back: Codon.

cards.front: Smallest of the four types of RNA?
cards.back: MicroRNA (miRNA).

cards.front: DNA dictates RNA through ____. RNA dictates protein through ____.
cards.back: Transcription. Translation.

cards.front: List 4 structural differences between DNA and RNA.
cards.back: Sugar (deoxyribose vs ribose), base (T vs U), strands (double vs usually single), job/location (stores info in nucleus vs protein synthesis, leaves nucleus).

cards.front: The concept of energy flow through living systems is called?
cards.back: Bioenergetics.

cards.front: All the chemical reactions inside cells (or an organism) is called?
cards.back: Metabolism.

cards.front: Equation for breaking down glucose?
cards.back: C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub> + 6O<sub>2</sub> → 6CO<sub>2</sub> + 6H<sub>2</sub>O + energy

cards.front: In photosynthesis, plants use sunlight to convert ____ into ____.
cards.back: CO<sub>2</sub> into sugar (glucose).

cards.front: Energy currency of the cell?
cards.back: ATP.

cards.front: What's needed to make 1 glucose from 6 CO<sub>2</sub>? How much ATP comes from breaking down 1 glucose?
cards.back: 18 ATP and 12 NADPH. 36 to 38 ATP.

cards.front: Pathways that require energy and build molecules are ____. Pathways that release energy and break molecules down are ____.
cards.back: Anabolic. Catabolic.

cards.front: The first organisms evolved ____ metabolism. Why?
cards.back: Anaerobic. The early atmosphere had no oxygen.

cards.front: Example of an anabolic pathway?
cards.back: Making sugar from CO<sub>2</sub> (photosynthesis), or building proteins from amino acids, or DNA from nucleotides.

cards.front: What type of protein facilitates each reaction step?
cards.back: An enzyme.

cards.front: Catabolic vs anabolic: give the energy, ergonic type, equation and memory trick for each.
cards.back: Catabolic: breaks down, releases energy, exergonic, AB → A + B + energy, "cats break things." Anabolic: builds, uses energy, endergonic, A + B → AB, "Anakin built the Death Star."

cards.front: How is energy defined? Energy of motion vs stored energy?
cards.back: The ability to do work. Kinetic vs potential.

cards.front: When a held ball drops, potential energy converts to ____. Potential energy in chemical bonds is called ____.
cards.back: Kinetic. Chemical energy.

cards.front: What is Gibbs free energy?
cards.back: Usable energy available to do work, after the energy lost to entropy is accounted for.

cards.front: During energy transfer, some energy becomes an unusable form such as ____.
cards.back: Heat.

cards.front: What is enthalpy? Formula for ΔG?
cards.back: The total energy change of the system (ΔH). ΔG = ΔH − TΔS.

cards.front: If energy is released, ΔG is ____ and the reaction is ____. If energy is required, ΔG is ____ and the reaction is ____.
cards.back: Negative, exergonic. Positive, endergonic.

cards.front: Anabolic processes are [endergonic / exergonic]. Catabolic are [endergonic / exergonic]. Which ones are spontaneous?
cards.back: Anabolic endergonic. Catabolic exergonic. Exergonic reactions are spontaneous.

cards.front: Example of an endergonic process from Fig 6.8?
cards.back: A chick developing from a fertilized egg.

cards.front: Two examples each of endergonic and exergonic reactions (quick reference).
cards.back: Endergonic: photosynthesis, melting ice. Exergonic: combustion, sodium + chlorine making table salt, chemiluminescence.

cards.front: True or false: most chemical reactions are reversible.
cards.back: True.

cards.front: The initial energy needed to start a reaction is the ____ energy. A contorted molecule about to break bonds is in the ____ state.
cards.back: Activation. Transition.

cards.front: Heating a system makes reactants react [faster / slower].
cards.back: Faster.

cards.front: Catalysts [raise / lower] activation energy. ΔG is [greater / less / unchanged] in catalyzed reactions.
cards.back: Lower. Unchanged.

cards.front: Thermodynamics is the study of ____.
cards.back: Energy and energy transfer involving matter.

cards.front: First law of thermodynamics?
cards.back: Energy can't be created or destroyed, only transferred or transformed (conservation of energy).

cards.front: Second law of thermodynamics (both ways the slide says it)?
cards.back: In a closed system, entropy (disorder) tends to increase over time. Or: heat flows from higher temperature to lower temperature.

cards.front: In the food chain slide, the plant gets 10 J from 1000 J of sunlight. Where did 990 J go, and which law explains it?
cards.back: Lost to the environment as heat. Second law (no transfer is 100% efficient). The first law says it wasn't destroyed.

cards.front: Heat energy is energy that transfers without ____. The amount of disorder in a system is ____.
cards.back: Doing work. Entropy.

cards.front: If entropy always increases, why don't living systems fall into chaos?
cards.back: They're open systems getting a constant input of energy, ultimately from the sun.

cards.front: Laws of thermodynamics, biology edition: three things organisms must do?
cards.back: (1) Obtain energy from surroundings (sun, food, chemicals). (2) Transform it into usable energy (ATP). (3) Lose some as heat during transfer.

cards.front: Five things living organisms need energy for?
cards.back: Metabolism, homeostasis, movement and activity, growth and development, reproduction.

cards.front: ATP is adenosine bound to ____. What reaction turns ATP into ADP + energy?
cards.back: Three phosphate groups. Hydrolysis.

cards.front: Energy coupling occurs in what process on the membrane?
cards.back: The sodium-potassium pump.

cards.front: What are enzymes made of? What do they do to activation energy?
cards.back: Proteins. Lower it.

cards.front: List the four properties of enzymes from the slide.
cards.back: Made of proteins; speed up reactions; unchanged after each reaction (reusable); specific to substrate.

cards.front: True or false: enzymes change ΔG of the reaction.
cards.back: False. They lower activation energy only.

cards.front: The reactants enzymes bind to are ____. The location where they bind is the ____.
cards.back: Substrates. Active site.

cards.front: True or false: enzymes are specific to their substrates. Enzymes are unchanged and reusable.
cards.back: True. True.

cards.front: What enzyme breaks down sucrose? Lactose? What ending do most enzyme names have?
cards.back: Sucrase. Lactase. -ase.

cards.front: Lactose is made of what two sugars joined by what bond? Where are the products absorbed?
cards.back: Galactose and glucose, glycosidic bond. Cells of the small intestine.

cards.front: How many subunits does lactase have, and what level of structure is that?
cards.back: 4 (1023 amino acids each, 4092 total). Quaternary.

cards.front: What is the induced fit model? How is it different from lock and key?
cards.back: Substrate and enzyme fit together, with the enzyme shifting shape slightly as the substrate binds. Lock and key is the older idea of a rigid, perfect fit. (Your slide calls them the same thing.)

cards.front: Degradation vs synthesis enzyme reactions?
cards.back: Degradation: substrate broken into smaller products. Synthesis: substrates combined into a larger product.

cards.front: Four factors that affect enzyme speed?
cards.back: Substrate concentration, temperature, pH, enzyme concentration.

cards.front: List three things that can increase the rate of an enzymatic reaction.
cards.back: More substrate, more enzyme, temperature or pH moved toward the optimum.

cards.front: What is the optimum temperature or pH?
cards.back: Where the enzyme has its fastest reaction rate.

cards.front: What can cause an enzyme to denature? What happens when it does?
cards.back: High temperature or extreme pH. It changes shape so much it no longer works (substrate can't bind).

cards.front: Why are Siamese cats darker on their nose and ears?
cards.back: Their enzyme tyrosinase only works at lower temperatures (below 33°C). Those body parts are cooler, so pigment is made there.

cards.front: Checkpoint: match A, B, C to X (change in free energy ΔG), Y (activation energy without enzyme), Z (activation energy with enzyme).
cards.back: A = Y (activation energy without enzyme, up to the black peak). B = Z (activation energy with enzyme, up to the red peak). C = X (ΔG, reactants down to products).

cards.front: On an energy graph, how can you tell exergonic from endergonic?
cards.back: Exergonic: products end lower than reactants (downhill). Endergonic: products end higher (uphill).

cards.front: Identify the type of inhibition for Enzyme A and Enzyme B.
cards.back: Enzyme A: competitive (inhibitor in the active site). Enzyme B: noncompetitive / allosteric (inhibitor on another site changes the shape).

cards.front: What is competitive inhibition?
cards.back: An inhibitor binds the active site and blocks the substrate.

cards.front: What is allosteric inhibition? Sketch it.
cards.back: An inhibitor binds a different site (allosteric site), changing the enzyme's shape so the substrate can't bind. Sketch: enzyme, inhibitor stuck on the side, active site warped, substrate not fitting.

cards.front: What is allosteric activation?
cards.back: An activator binds the allosteric site and changes the enzyme's shape so it binds substrate more efficiently.

cards.front: What is feedback inhibition? Which enzyme does the product block on the slide?
cards.back: The product of a pathway inhibits an enzyme in that pathway, slowing or stopping more product. It blocks enzyme 1 (at its allosteric site).

cards.front: How are enzymes regulated? (Checkpoint Q5)
cards.back: Competitive inhibitors, allosteric inhibitors, allosteric activators, feedback inhibition (plus temperature and pH).

cards.front: Most common source of coenzymes?
cards.back: Dietary vitamins.

cards.front: Relationship between enzymes and thermodynamics? (Checkpoint Q6)
cards.back: Enzymes lower activation energy so reactions go faster, but they don't change ΔG, so they can't make an endergonic reaction spontaneous. They aren't used up.

cards.front: How can you see catalase working? Write the equation.
cards.back: Bubbling oxygen. 2H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> → 2H<sub>2</sub>O + O<sub>2</sub>

cards.front: Two ways to measure amylase activity?
cards.back: Measure the maltose produced from starch, or use iodine to test whether starch is still present.

cards.front: Two ways to measure the speed of an enzyme reaction?
cards.back: Measure how much product is made (oxygen), or how much substrate (H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>) is left when you stop it.

cards.front: Why does the oxygen-produced graph level off?
cards.back: The substrate (hydrogen peroxide) got used up.

cards.front: Yeast-lactose experiment: purpose of the balloons, what goes in the control, IV and DV?
cards.back: Balloons catch CO<sub>2</sub> (shows how much sugar the yeast used). Control: yeast + water, no sugar. IV: type of sugar (and lactase added or not). DV: CO<sub>2</sub> produced (balloon size).

cards.front: Yeasts are what kind of organism, and what do they produce from sugar?
cards.back: Single-celled fungi, heterotrophs. CO<sub>2</sub>.

cards.front: Essential questions: what allows milk digestion, and why can some adults still do it?
cards.back: Lactase hydrolyzes lactose into glucose and galactose in the small intestine. Lactase-persistent adults keep making lactase after infancy.

cards.front: What happens in a lactose-intolerant person's gut?
cards.back: Lactose isn't broken down, reaches the large intestine, and bacteria ferment it into gas and acids: diarrhea, pain, gas, bloating.

cards.front: List the levels of organization in order from smallest (atom) to largest (biosphere).
cards.back: Atom → molecule → cell → tissue → organ → organ system → organism → population → community → ecosystem → biosphere.

cards.front: In the sequence subatomic particles → atoms → molecules → cells → tissues → organs → organ systems, why is the cell the most important level?
cards.back: The cell is the smallest level that is alive. Atoms and molecules are not alive; cells are the smallest unit that can carry out all the characteristics of life.

cards.front: What is the difference between a population and a community? Between a community and an ecosystem?
cards.back: Population = one species in an area. Community = all the different populations (species) living together in an area. Ecosystem = the community plus the nonliving physical environment (water, soil, air).

cards.front: Name the three domains and the six kingdoms. Sort the six kingdoms into their domains.
cards.back: Domains: Bacteria, Archaea, Eukarya. Kingdoms: Eubacteria (Bacteria), Archaebacteria (Archaea), and Protista, Plantae, Fungi, Animalia (all Eukarya).

cards.front: What is LUCA? Who defined the Archaea, when, and what technique did he use?
cards.back: LUCA = last universal common ancestor, the root of the tree of life. Carl Woese defined the Archaea in 1977 using phylogenetic taxonomy of 16S ribosomal RNA.

cards.front: List the 7 levels of taxonomy in order with the memory trick. Then give the full classification of the leopard (Panthera pardus) at every level.
cards.back: Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species ("King Philip Came Over For Great Soup"). Leopard: Animalia, Chordata, Mammalia, Carnivora, Felidae, Panthera, Panthera pardus.

cards.front: In the kingdoms Plantae and Fungi, which taxonomic level replaces "phylum"?
cards.back: Division.

cards.front: What is the smallest unit of matter? Name its three particles, their charges, and where each is found.
cards.back: The atom. Protons (+) and neutrons (no charge) are in the nucleus. Electrons (−) orbit around the nucleus in shells (orbitals).

cards.front: Define atomic number and atomic mass. On the periodic table, oxygen's box shows 8, O, Oxygen and 15.999. What do the 8 and the 15.999 stand for?
cards.back: Atomic number = number of protons. Atomic mass = number of protons + neutrons. 8 = atomic number; 15.999 = atomic mass. (O is the chemical symbol, Oxygen is the element name.)

cards.front: Describe a Bohr model of oxygen (atomic number 8, mass 16): what is in the nucleus, and how many electrons are in each shell?
cards.back: Nucleus: 8 protons and 8 neutrons. Inner shell: 2 electrons. Outer shell: 6 electrons.

cards.front: Give three uses of radioisotopes.
cards.back: PET (positron emission tomography) scans to diagnose disease; radiation therapy to treat certain cancers; carbon-14 decay for carbon dating. (PET and radiation therapy are part of nuclear medicine.)

cards.front: What is the maximum number of electrons in the inner shell? In outer shells? Which electrons interact with other atoms, and what two things can they do?
cards.back: Inner shell: max 2. Outer shells: max 8. The outer shell electrons interact with other atoms. They can be shared (covalent) or donated/transferred (ionic).

cards.front: What is the difference between a covalent bond and an ionic bond?
cards.back: Covalent bond: electrons are shared between atoms. Ionic bond: electrons are transferred from one atom to another, making charged ions that attract.

cards.front: What happens to the electrons when sodium and chlorine form NaCl? What is the charge on each ion afterward?
cards.back: Sodium transfers (gives) 1 electron to chlorine. Sodium becomes Na+ and chlorine becomes Cl−. The opposite charges attract: an ionic bond.

cards.front: What does a single line vs a double line mean in a structure drawing? Give an example of a molecule with a double bond.
cards.back: Single line = single bond (one shared pair). Double line = double bond (two shared pairs). O2 has a double bond (nonpolar covalent double bond).

cards.front: What is the difference between the covalent bonds inside a water molecule and the hydrogen bonds between water molecules?
cards.back: Covalent bonds hold the H's to the O inside one water molecule (shared electrons, strong). Hydrogen bonds are weak attractions between the δ+ H of one water molecule and the δ− O of a neighboring water molecule.

cards.front: List the 7 properties (characteristics) of life.
cards.back: Order, response to stimuli, reproduction, growth and development, regulation, homeostasis, energy processing.

cards.front: What does "order" mean as a property of life? Write the sequence of order from subatomic particles up to organ systems.
cards.back: Living things are highly organized. Subatomic particles → atoms → molecules → cells → tissues → organs → organ systems.

cards.front: Define regulation and homeostasis. What does the word homeostasis literally mean?
cards.back: Regulation: internal functions are coordinated within systems (groups of organs working together). Homeostasis: maintaining a stable internal environment (dynamic equilibrium). Homeo = same, stasis = state.

cards.front: Homeostasis means maintaining a dynamic equilibrium. What does "dynamic" mean here? Give four things the body keeps in homeostasis.
cards.back: Dynamic means the body is constantly adjusting to changes in the environment; it's not a fixed state. Examples: temperature, blood sugar, threats, food availability.

cards.front: What does ghrelin do? What does leptin do and when is it released?
